speechtext: That the provisions of rule 60 requiring twenty-four hours' notice of private Bills originating in the Senate before being considered by the committee of this House to which they are referred, be suspended for the remainder of the session.
BORDEN (Halifax) What is the particular reason for this ?
A number of Bills usually come from the Senate at a late stage of the session, and if such a motion as this is not adopted, they cannot be considered at all.

The difficulty is that persons who may desire to be heal'd with regard to these Bills will have no opportunity of presenting their views before the committee. A case of that kind was brought to my notice this morning. A Bill is on the Order paper for the second reading to-night, and if this motion be adopted, it will go to the committee to-morrow morning, and it would be impossible to arrange that persons who wish to be heard with regard to that Bill should be present. However great may be the desire to close the session on a particular day, that must not be carried so far as to prevent those who are interested in these matters from being heard. I am as much desirous as any other gentleman to have our labours terminated at an early date, but we cannot do

that at the expense of denying these people the right to be heard. I can only assent to the motion on the understanding that sufficient time will be given to parties interested to place their views before the committee.

1 do not think that any injustice will be done to any person if this motion passes. If representations were made that the parties interested in a Rill desired to be heard, no committee would think of pressing that Bill forward under this rule if injustice were to be done. We sometimes forget in dealing with business of a public nature that these Bills of incorporation and other private Bills are of the utmost importance to those interested in them, and that every opportunity should be given to have them passed before prorogation. This is an ordinary motion which is made near the end of each session.
speakername: The MINISTER OP MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. James Sutherland).

speechtext: I am not much in favour of suspending the rules of the House, except for very urgent reasons. This motion seems to have been usual in the past, and I shall not object to it at present, provided it is distinctly understood that it shall only apply to Bills which are not opposed, and that Bills which are opposed shall be suspended for a sufficient length of time to give reasonable facilities to those who desire to be heard in opposition.

There can be no objection to that understanding.
Motion was agreed to.

Before the Orders of the Day are called, I would like to Inform the government, particularly the hon. Minister of the Interior, that I have received a further communication from the miners whose telegram I read in the House the other day, asking for a reply to the message which was then sent, respecting the Miller Creek concession. speechtext: House in Committee on Bill (No. 134) respecting the representation of the Yukon Territory in the House of Commons.-The Minister of the Interior.

I wish to move a few small changes in the Bill. There are two slight changes in section 8. to improve the wording, and to make the meaning clear.
I have been furnished with a copy of tl;e amendments suggested by my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster). The most of these amendments I see no objection to, but there is one which involves a radical change In the principle of appointment, and which we would have to debate. I would suggest that we first go through the Act and make the clerical amendments I suggest, after having carefully examined and revised the clauses. Then we will go back and take up my hon. friend's amendments one after the other.
speakername: The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR (Hon. Clifford Sifton).

speechtext:
That will be all right, it being understood that we have the same rights exactly as if we had not gone through the Bill.
The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR moved that section 18 be amended by inserting after the word * Canada ' in the forty-fifth line, ' or a cheque for that amount accepted by such bank.' This is to make the Act accord with the change in the law by which a certified cheque may be accepted as deposit.
Amendment agreed to.

The sections 40, 41 and 42 provide for a man being placed on the list on polling day after he lias taken the oath. I may say that that principle was not in the North-west Territories Representation Act, but an amendment was subsequently passed providing that that might be done. I do not think that It will work satisfactorily in the territories. Hon. gentlemen will agree with me that in a place like the Yukon, where there is a

large floating population, it is desirable that the list should be final, and that upon election day an election should not be capable of being influenced by a large number of persons who might come to the poll and simply take the oath. The original Northwest Territories Representation Act did uot make any such provision, but provided that the lists should be final.
1 n 1899 an amendment was passed, at whose instance I do not know, authorizing persons to vote on taking the oath upon election day. I know that at the last general election that Was found to be unsatisfactory. Persons were unaware whether they had the right to vote or not and where they could vote, and, generally there was a lack of certainty about what the rights of the voters are which always arises when the list is not final. Parliament has decided many times that whatever disadvantages there may be about having a voters' list, one of the great advantages is that when it is made up and fairly revised, it .is final.
How long before election day would the voters' list be considered to be final ?
The list is made up pending the election, after the proclamation is issued; and, when the voters' list 'is completed as provided in the Act, it is final.

How many days before the election, does the final revision take place ?
The MINISTER OP THE INTERIOR, No change can be made later than two days before the election, according to the present Bill as it is drawn. In that it follows the provisions of the old North-west Territories Act. That is not a matter to which I am wedded. If it is desired to make it longer, I would li'ave no objection. But I am quite clear in my mind that it is not at all desirable that after the list is made up, and on election day, persons would have the right to vote simply on taking an affidavit. For, in that ease, you might as well have no voters' 'list at all. I regret to say that we cannot always depend, as much as we would like to do, upon the indisposition of persons whom we should be able to trust, to take an oath that is not true. So I will ask the committee to amend these sections. I furnished my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax), with a copy of the amendment to section 41, but, as it did not seem to be very well drawn I have changed it slightly. It is as follows
la case any person whose name is on the list refuses to take either of the said oaths, erasing lines shall be drawn through his name on the voters' list and the words ' refused to be awcrn ' written thereafter, and such person whose name is so erased shall not be permitted to vote.

It would be better to say ' shall not be permitted to vote at said election,' to make it perfectly Hon. Mr. SiFTON.
clear that it does not apply to any subsequent election.
All right.
Amendment agreed to.

I move that section 42 be amended to read as follows :-
Every voter shall he entitled to vote whose name is on the voters' list and has not been erased therefrom in accordance with the foregoing provisions of this Act.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) The territory covered ,by this Bill is a very large one. How is it possible for the returning officer to ge,t correct lists if the final corrections in the list are made only two days before tbe election ?

The system was worked out in the Northwest Territories with especial reference to the fact that there 'is an enumerator for each polling division. The list is not necessarily sent back to the returning officer for the whole constituency and by him returned to the deputy returning otficer, but is made up by the enumerator for each polling subdivision.
Amendments agreed to.

I have no objection to tlie principle at all. I would just say in reference to this amendment, that tlie Bill was carefully gone through by Mr. Ross, the commissioner, when be was here, and there were a number of changes made to suit the local circumstances of tbe case. Mr. Ross assured me that he was perfectly satisfied with it after he had revised it. The question of the publication of the notice, I think, was sufficiently considered, and he was satisfied that the provision was all right. The hon. gentleman will notice'that there is a change made in the usual method, by providing that notice shall be published in the newspapers, and I presume that Mr. Ross thought that would be quite sufficient. I have not the least objection to the hon. gentleman's suggestion if he thinks it will be safer to have fifty notices posted up.

I think it would he necessary, for the reason that without this
4470

amendment nobody In the district would have any chance of knowing anything- about the election going on, unless he saw the notice in one of the daily newspapers published at Dawson, or in the daily newspaper published at White Horse. It' lie did not see it in the newspaper published at White Horse or Dawson, he would have no opportunity of knowing that an election was about to be held, and I am inclined to think, in view of what the hon. minister has said, that he did not think of that fact, and as the hon. minister sees no objection to the amendment, I think it ought to be adopted.

I think it is hardly safe to put in the words 1 in all parts,' because the electoral district is the whole Yukon district. It would be absolutely impossible to get these notices into all parts, because there are inaccessible parts, but, the hon. gentleman mignt make it more general, and use these words : ' to ensure notice generally throughout the said electoral district.'
That would be better, because it would be a hard matter to have these notices distributed throughout that country.

It might be a very hard matter, as the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Ross) suggests, but it would also be a very hard matter if the voters in these districts should not get notice. They are the people who elect the representatives. Of course, I do not think you would be bound to post notices in the wilderness.
Suppose you say : ' to ensure notice generally through the said electoral district ' ?

How would it do to say that these notices should be put up at the post offices ? Surely there would be a post office wherever there would be any number of people to vote. Suppose they were sent to the postmasters, and the postmasters were ordered to put them up.

The objection to that would be that the postmasters might not do it. This is a distribution of responsibility which is very unsafe. I think that the hon. minister will agree with me that we are right in keeping the responsibility confined to as few people as possible, because the moment we distribute the responsibility we lose tlie benefit of the provision. The postmasters might not put them up, or they might not put them up in sufficient time to give the necessary notice. If the hon. minister thinks the language I propose a little too strong, I would suggest that we use these words : ' to ensure notice to all parts of tlie said electoral district where there are voters.' Wherever there are voters they should have a chance to know that an election is about to be held.

That will do ; but I want to make sure that
we are not putting in a provision that would be impracticable. Suppose there were ten or twenty voters who had gone on an expedition 500 miles away to an inaccessible part, you would then run tlie risk of having Cue election declared void if it were brought before the court. What we should do is to use words that the court will give a construction to that we want it to give. We want the court, if this comes up for construction, to say that the notice must have been put up bona fide, so as to give what we all consider to be proper notice. We ought not to use any words which will compel the court to hold something which will be contrary to common sense. Suppose we say : ' At sufficient distance from each other to ensure general and sufficient notice throughout the said electoral district.'
I think that would do.
With that, I will agree to the amendment. Perhaps wre had better go through the amendments and discuss them before changing the Bill.
Perhaps I had better insert these words suggested by the hon. minister : ' To ensure general and sufficient notice throughout tlie said electoral district.'
I think before changing the Bill we had better discuss the various amendments, and we can then come back and change the sections that we decide to amend.

And I also propose to amend section 16, by adding the following words : ' and shall give the same notice on the day fixed for such later nomination in the newspapers, and by proclamation, as is required by section 15 of this Act.'
There is no objection to that ; but I am doubtful about the next one.
I propose that section 17 shall be amended by striking out the word ' four,' in the third line of said section, and inserting instead thereof the word ' twenty-five.'

I do not think that it would be well to make it twenty-five. Twenty-five is the number provided for in the general Act. The hon. gentleman has not lived in a sparsely settled district. I have seen cases, for instance in Manitoba, where a candidate came very nearly not getting his nomination paper in because he had very great difficulty getting a sufficient number of voters to sign it on the last day. I remember once being very nearly not being able to get my own nomination paper signed. It was left until the last two or three days. I was away, and my agent was away, and it was very difficult. It was a rural district ; there were no towns in the district, and a man had to

[DOT]drive from one farmer's. house to another getting their signatures. It was a tremendous job, and took two days, and we just barely got the nomination paper signed in time. In a sparsely settled district the number should not be placed too high. I have no [DOT]objection to having it placed at fifteen.
We had better say 15. Four is so few that it Is hardly a proper nomination.
Make it 15.	.
Amendment agreed to.

I move to amend section 25 toy adding at the end thereof :
Each polling division shall contain not less than 100 and not more than 200 qualified voters.
There is nothing in the Bill which says what shall be the number of voters in each polling place, and while I do not pretend to say that the number in the amendment is the most desirable number, yet I think a maximum and a minimum should be provided.

The idea is quite right, but I think that the minimum limit mentioned by the hon. gentleman is too high. There may be groups of miners at a distance where it would be necessary to have a polling place, and perhaps if the minimum were fixed at 25 it would meet the case. Of course in a closely settled place like Dawson city, the maximum might be put at 200 or even 300.
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax) What is the minimum in the General Election Act ?
200, but 400 or 500 could vote quite easily in a day in a polling place.

Probably the minister has not been scrutineer so often as I have, and I know that it takes a good while to count 200 votes' If there is any delay because of objection to the voters, or because of swearing them, there is difficulty in polling even 200 in the one booth.

On general principles I am in favour of the maximum being 400 or 500 instead of 200, because it saves expense, and under the present law we have too many polling booths throughout the country. In Dawson city the maximum might be 300, but in other districts in such a country as that you might not have more than 15 who could vote at the one polling place, and I would certainly not be in favour of disfranchising them. Perhaps a provision could be made that in sparsely settled districts the minimum would be so much, and in thickly populated districts so much.

It would be hardly desirable to hold a poll unless you have at least 25 voters. I have not bi'en a scrutineer perhaps so often as my hon. friend (Mr. Lancaster), but I have been around polling booths since I was 15 Hon. Mr. SIFTON.
years old, and I have never yet seen a case where a voter could not vote if he was there to vote.
It must be remembered that if there are 300 voters' names on the list, probably not more than 220 will vote.
We will make the minimum 25, and the maximum 200.
Amendment agreed to.

I beg to move to amend section 20 by adding the following subsection.
The proclamation of the granting of such poll shall be published for at least two weeks preceding the taking of such poll, In the newspapers and by posting up as provided by section 15 of this Act.
That is all right.
Amendment agreed to.

I beg to move to amend section 27 :
By inserting after the word ' election ' in the third line, the words ' and in twelve other of the most conspicuous polling places in each polling division.'
There should be a posting up at some other places than at the polling booth.
Say four places instead of twelve.
Very well. Amendment agreed to.

The government 'have no objection at all to the principle that ,fhe Chief Justice or the senior Judge of the Territory shall appoint the enumerators. We do not desire to retain that power in our hands. Therefore, so far as the principle of the amendment is concerned, we concede it at once. But I do not think my hon. friend is correct in saying that liis other amendments depend on this one. I think it is the other way. My hon. friend wants this change made so that the making-up of the list shall be taken out of the bands of the government and put into the hfinds of an independent tribunal. That being the case, lie does not require the same precautions respecting the making-up of the list. In the old North-west Territories Act, which my hon. friend will remember was passed by his friends, and under which we laboured at some disadvantage for a number of years, the Governor In Council appointed the enumerator to make the lists, and he required no affidavit, no evidence, and there was no appeal of any kind what' ever from his decisions.
That is as this Bill is without this amendment.
That was the most remarkable Act ever passed in Canada.
We have that in Ontario.
No, you have a revising officer, and you have a right of appeal.

Not for a list of this character. The hon. minister is referring
to the old form of municipal lists ; but we also have a registration of voters, largely on this line, in cities and towns.

Under the old North-west Territories Act, which in a general way we are following in this Bill, the Governor in Council appointed the enumerators, and there was no revision. I admit that that is not a fair position for any political party to occupy ; and for that reason I do not think my hon. friend is unreasonable in asking that a judicial officer like the Chief Justice or the senior Judge of the Territory should appoint the enumerators. But I wish to point out to my hon. friend that in the clause he has drawn he has followed the idea that the lists are to be made up every year, while tlie scheme of the Act is that the lists should only be made up for an election and I do not want to depart from that. I am content to accept my hon. friend's suggestion ; but I would not be satisfied that we had the provisions in a satisfactory, workable shape, by just drawing them here hurriedly.

Let me make a suggestion to the hon. gentleman. In the Ontario Registration Act, it is provided that seven days after the dissolution of parliament the registrars shall he called for the purpose of preparing a list of those entitled to register. In this Bill it could be provided that the registration should take place within seven days after tihe issue of the writ or at some other specified time.

That is exactly wffiat the scheme of the Act is at present. This section provides that the lists shall be made up immediately after the issue of the writ.
I will accept my hon. friend's suggestion that the Chief Justice or senior judge should designate the enumerators, but I think we should retain the scheme of this Act and provide that he should designate the enumerators within a certain number of days, and be notified to do so at the same time that the writ is sent to the returning officer.
I am satisfied to accept the hon. gentleman's suggestion. His idea is that the Chief Justice or senior judge should be appointed to designate the enumerators instead of the Governor in Council.
If we agree on that, I presume my hon. friend will not insist on the subsequent amendment requiring an affidavit for qualification.

I think I ought to insist on that because tbe Chief Justice ought to have some rule oh -which he is to proceed. AVe should define what sort of evidence he must take. In other provinces there must be a declaration or personal attendance and swearing. There should be some rule of evidence to guide the Chief Justice and the enumerators in the matter. There is one thing I do not understand. How is the hon.

minister going to fix the day for doing this? If you wait until the writ is issued, you will never have time enough to properly register these people. There is this difference between my proposition and the hon. minister's. He begins to count from a date unknown. He begins to count back from the election, while I am trying to fix some day before the election and do everything from that time forward, and if there should be a little time between the completion of the lists and polling day that will not do any harm. But if you begin so many days from the day of polling, and should not toe able to get through with the work toy polling day you will have chaos and trouble. I am glad the hon. minister accepts my suggestion that the Chief Justice should appoint the enumerators, but I would like to know when the Chief Justice will begin to do that. Would it not toe well for him to do it on the first of August this year ?
Wo [DOT]cannot work that.
The Chief Justice should know when he has to appoint these enumerators, and unless we fix a special time, how is he to know it ?

How would it do to send a notice to the senior judge, immediately on sending the writs to the returning officer, and provide that he should immediately commence having the lists made up, and have them completed within say three months of the receipt of such notice. That would be fixing a definite date at which the list would toe completed. In your writ you could say that the nomination would take place a fortnight or a month after the completion of the lists. That would give ample opportunity for the lists to be properly completed. You could provide that the Chief Justice, say three months from the time he gets his notice, shall have the list completed, and then in the writ fix the date of nomination one month after the lists are completed.

We have to do one of two things. We have to decide on an annual list or a list for the election. There is no middle course. We must have the one thing or the other. I think the committee will admit that it would toe quite unnecessary and useless to *have an annual list. The hon. gentleman knows from experience under the late Dominion Franchise Act that when people did not think there was going to toe an election they did not register, and some times the elections came on when the lists were very imperfect. The proper principle is to have the lists made up for the election. The one thing we have to decide is what shall be the period when the judge shall appoint enumerators who will set to work and make up the lists.

Is it the intention of the ..government to have the elections .in the Yu-Mr. LANCASTER.
kon on the same day as the general elections throughout the Dominion ?
The general elections, certainly.

I was going to suggest a way out of the difficulty if the government did not intend doing that. If the general elections in the Yukon would take place at a certain time after the general elections in the Dominion, the lists could then be prepared, because every one would know that the elections would take place three, or six months after the general elections in the Dominion. That would do away with the expense of the annual lists and give ample time for making up the list before the elections, and no advantage would accrue to either party other than that which of course falls, especially in a district like the Yukon, to the party elected to power.

The trouble is that that does not get over the difficulty. The Election Act should provide for the different contingencies that may arise. We wish to provide machinery for holding the first election; and, in case the member who is elected should unfortunately die, we want it in such shape that we can hold another election. We want to get back to the same point and decide what should initiate proceedings, and I think the initiation of proceedings! must be. the issue of the writ. The Governor in Council muslt decide when the writ shall issue, and we can work out the rest of it very simply by providing that rwheu the writ is issued, notice shall toe sent to the Chief Justice and he shall order that the lists shall toe made up.

If the minister will say that they will issue the writ in time for these things to toe done, that is a good way to fix the date. But you wiill have to issue the writ a good while before the election.	.
I will submit the draft to my hon. friend. We cannot make the amendment this morning, because I must have the law clerk examine the draft and see that the duties dovetail in correctly.

In the next section, No. 29, I move in amendment that the word ' immediately ' toe struck out. And the words ' within thirty days ' be inserted instead thereof. The word ' immediately ' seemed to me too wide; it is construed in all kinds of ways toy judges and others. The enumerator, to do his work properly, should be limited to a certain time. He can do it the next day, if he wishes, tout tins provides a limit of thirty day's. He might think that ' immediately ' in the Yukon would mean two or three months.
The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR
I do not see any objection to the amendment.

I move Hint this section, No. 29, be amended toy adding tlie following subsection :
(a) In the compilation of such list the enumerator may only enter therein the names of such person or persons as appear upon the last revised list or shall by statutory declaration filed with him' be declared, by such person or some agent having a personal knowledge of the facts declared to, to possess the qualifications necessary to entitle him' to vote under the provisions of this Act.

I do not tlrink that * the last revised list ' should have anything to do with it. In a constituency such as this, where the people are shifting continually, the last revised list will have the names of a great many people who have left the district; -and, in order to get their names off it will be necessary to prove that they have left. There should be an absolutely new list for each election.

I might explain that 1 intend to propose amendments later on which will allow striking names off the list. The reason I have worded it in tlie way I have is this-if a man knows that he was on the list last year, and is still a resident, he would not unnaturally suppose that he is still on the list. And so, even in the absence of bis own declaration or iu the absence of some agent, it' would not be wrong for the officer to leave his name there. I propose to make provision that if his name should be struck off, it can be done on application to the Chief Justice.

I have had a good deal to do with the revision of the voters' list, and imy experience is that at is a good deal more difficult to get names off than to get them on. If we had a system of registration, we could do as they do throughout the whole of the United States. There, when an election is to Ibe held, everybody has <to reglister irrespective of whether his name was on the voters' list or not. And no matter who a man anay be, even if lie is the greatest millionaire in the country, if he is a congressman or senator, he must register if hei wishes to vote. In the Yukon, we should adopt a system similar to that, and the voters' list should be made up absolutely new.

I would like to suggest to tbe minister and my hon. friend from Lincoln and Niagara (Mr. Lancaster) that, perhaps, it would be better to word that section in some such way as this :	1 Such enumerator, upon liis appointment, and having first taken the oath of office shall, immediately thereafter proceed to compile and within thirty days shall complete '-and so on. To leave the word ' compile ' alone might possibly create a little uncertainty.
I have no objection.
That is what my hon. friend (Mr. Lancaster) intended, I think.

But, perhaps it expresses it a little more distinctly.
4 Mr. GOURLEY'. I think that thirty days is too short. In a big district like the Yukon, it 'Should be at least ninety, days. Let tlie compilation begin immediately, and be finished within ninety days.

But ithe hon. gentleman (Mr. Gourley) must not forget that the intention of that Act is that each polling subdivision shall have an enumerator whose duty it shall he to prepare the list for the polling subdivision.
But some of the residents may be two hundred aniles away.

It does not make any differenc if they are two thousand miles away. A polling division is to contain not lsss than twenty-five or more than two hundred electors^ The, eaiumeraltor lias thirty days within which to make the list, and it does not make any difference if the constituency stretches for ten thousand miles beyond ithe limits of the polling sub divisions-the enumerator has onily to do with his own pant of it. We must avoid the mistake we are making in Ontario where we have the registration system in our cities and county towns. We have not sufficient time in Ontario for the registration, and that is the curse of -the system. We want to have the lists in the Yukon completed a sufficiently long time before tbe election for the people to know who have votes and who have not. That, I take it, is the object desired by the leader of the opposition and the member for Lancaster and Niagara.

The objection I raise had nothing to do with the size of the constituency, but with the size of the polling division. Have a clause, providing, that not less than thirty or sixty days after your lists are completed, the writs are to be issued and the election take place. But I would say two months. What my learned friend says is very just, that lin a town or small district in Ontario, thirty days would be enough. But no matter whether there is an enumerator appointed for every electoral district in tlhe Yukon or not, I fancy many electoral districts will be more thaii 200 miles in extent. I have lived in the North-west, and I know that electors may be 50 or 100 miles apart; and how is ail enumerator to make up his list and give people an opportunity, in thirty days to come to the court ? Half of them would never know there was an enumerator appointed, and half of them would never know it was their duty to go to that enumerator within thirty days. You want sixty or ninety days.

It is quite immaterial whether we send the writs to the returning officer and at the same time send a notice to the judge, or whether you send a notice to the judge and two

months after send the writs to the returning officer.
It ought to be GO days anyhow.
I do not see how we can work these other amendments respecting an appeal.

The minister means that there would not be time for the appeals.
The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR There would not be time, it would be wholly impossible. We give you all the protection we can ; we give you the appointment of the enumerator by the chief justice, and then we give the protection that nobody can go on the list unless there is an affidavit filed.

In section 30, the amendment I propose would he all right. It does not deal with the appeal, but it makes the chief justice the custodian of the lists. My amendment to section 30 requires the enumerator to have ten days after completing such list instead of retaining them to deliver them to the chief justice. So the chief justice is the custodian.

As it is now, the list must be completed eight days before polling day. The hon gentleman thinks that is not long enough, and.that the time should be longer between the completion of the list and the polling. I think so to.
How many days would you suggest ?

I should think 30 days at least would be best in that country.
The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR, You are not going to get much by that unless you have a general revision.

Only this. If you crowd the work of completing the list, if the time is too short, then you are working at a disadvantage. But if you would have ample time, 30 days will be long enough. In Ontario we have not ample time, the work is crowded. There is much time devoted to the preparation of the lists that both parties would rather use in some other way.

I have no objection to the period between the completion of the list and the election being made longer than two days. I think perhaps it might be desirable that the lists should be completed and everybody should know who had a right to vote, for a longer period than two days. But it is to be remembered that the enumerator appointed by the chief justice shall both make up and revise the list. So there is no object in having a longer period of time. The object in having a longer period of time in other places is to permit that revision to take place. But in this case it is the enumerator appointed by the chief justice who revises

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

No matter whether the enumerator makes up the list or not, every man in the electoral district wants to know of it, and wants to have time to get there. Bill (No. 154) to amend the Naturalization Act (the Prime Minister) read the second time and House went into committee thereon.

The only object of this Bill is to provide that a record shall be kept in the Department of the Secretary of State at Ottawa of all naturalization papers which are granted in Canada. As a rule, naturalization papers are easily obtained and easily lost, and no list is kept of them. Certificates are granted by the courts of the different provinces which are authorized to grant naturalization papers, and the Bill provides that the clerks of those courts shall be required to send lists of all these papers to the Department of the Secretary of State, where access may be had to them at all times.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: As the preparation of some of these lists extending back over a considerable number of years would involve considerable labour to the officers of the courts whose duty it is to prepare them, would it not be advisable to provide what fees shall be paid to these officers ?

We have thought of that. It would not be possible at present to form an accurate idea of what it would cost; but if there is money to be disbursed, we think it can be taken from the fund provided for the purposes of the Act.
I understand it is a matter which is to be taken into consideration ?

Yes.
Bill reported; read the third time, and passed.

The leader of the opposition has given notice of a couple of amendments. The first is that ordinances passed by the Governor in Council should not remain in force longer than the end of the next ensuing session unless approved by resolution of both Houses of parliament. 1 can see no special objection to the principle of that amendment, and am quite prepared to accept it.

My hon. friend has also given notice of another amendment, bnt which is really an amendment to the Dominion Lands Act. 1 presume what he desires is practically to limit the operation of the regulations and ordinances relating to mining under the Dominion Lands Act in the same way as the amendment I have just referred to limits ordinances applicable to the Yukon passed by the Governor in Council. We might insert a clause which would have the effect of operating this restriction as regards the Yukon Territory, but could hardly pass it in this Bill as of general application. If the hon. gentleman will accept my suggestion, I am satisfied.
speakername: The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR (Hon. Clifford Sifton).

speechtext: What the hon. gentleman suggests is perfectly relevant as regards this Bill, though we have ample precedents in the past, even under this administration, for introducing sections of somewhat general application in measures of more limited application. As the territory of the Yukon is altogether the subject of this Bill, I would be disposed to accept the suggestion of the hon. gentleman and have the second amendment limited in its operation to the Yukon Territory.

Then, we will accept the first as drawn. The best way, I think, to reach the object of the second amendment would be to insert a new section as section 5 of this Bill, and I beg to submit one which I have rather hurriedly drawn :
Every regulation made by the Governor in Council, under section 5 of the Dominion Lands Act, chapter 54 of the revised statutes of Canada as amended, applicable to the Yukon Territory, shall remain1 in force until the day immediately succeeding the day of prorogation. Then we may continue with the rest of the amendment ns proposed by my hon. friend. With regard to section 3, considered In connection with the typewritten amendments, of which I furnished the hon. gentleman a copy, in line 38 of the Bill, section 3, it will be seen that the words ' or commissioners in council ' are found. Those words were put in when the original Bill was drawn l*y the late Minister of Justice, because under this section there was a restriction of the power to make ordinances, preventing the commissioner In council imposing taxes. This was done because the commissioners in council were not a body representing the people, but an appointed body. Now, however, they are a representative body, to the extent that half their members are representatives, and under section 2 they have the same powers as the assembly of the North-west Territories. I think, therefore, it would he well to strike out the latter part of ithe amendment at first proposed. This section will apply only to Acts by the Governor in Council ; and leave off the last section of the typewritten amendment which relates to the power of 1414
the commissioner in council. So, I will ask my hon. Mend to follow me as I read the section as it would be :
Section 8 of the said Act, as that section is enacted by section 2 of chapter 11 of the statutes of 1899, is repealed and the following is substituted therefor :
'8. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the Governor in Council may make ordinances for the peace, order, and good government of the territory, and of His Majesty's subjects anu others therein ; but no ordinance made by the Governor in Council shall- .
' (a.) tor the enforcement of any ordinance, impose any penalty exceeding five hundred dollars ;
' (b) alter or repeal the punishment provided in any Act of the parliament of Canada in force in the territory for any offence ;
'(c.) appropriate any public land or other property of Canada without authority of parliament, or impose any duty of customs or any excise.'
Nor shall any tax be imposed except as under this Act provided.
Provided always that the Governor in Council may make ordinances.
(a)	Imposing a tax or royalty upon gold and silver the output of the mines in the territory.
(b)	Prescribing and regulating the place and manner of collection of such tax or royalty and the method of securing and enforcing the payment thereof.
(cl Provide for the confiscation and forfeiture of gold and silver upon which such tax or royalty has not been paid, as well as for the confiscation and forfeiture of any vessel, vehicle, ear or other receptacle containing the same or used or intended to be used for the transportation thereof ; and,
(d) Giving to any officer of the Crown, in respect of searches, examinations and other proceedings for the enforcement of the provisions of any such ordinances, such powers, rights, privileges and protection as the Governor in Council, may think necessary or desirable in that behalf.
Thus, the commissioner in council's authority will come under section 2, exclusively, while the Governor in Council's authority will come under section 3, exclusively, and there will be no chance of confusion.

I am disposed to think that I would not suggest any further amendment, but I would like time for consideration. I would ask the hon. gentleman to let the matter stand over until this evening. Meantime, I will look the amendment over, and if I have any suggestion to offer, I will have it ready then.

House again in committee on Bill (No. 162) to amend the Manitoba Grain Act, 1900.
On section 1,

Before that clause is adopted, I have a few remarks which 1 wish to make and some amendments to the Bill to suggest, which amendments I may explain now, and they can be dealt with more particularly as we take up the sections to

which they relate. But the first complaint that we have to make with regard to this Bill is that the very important amendments pi'oposed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce come before us so late in the session that it is almost impossible properly to discuss them. Within a few days of the beginning of the session, I drew the attention of the government to this very important measure. Yet it is not until now, within four or five days of the close of this session, that this measure, which is the most important on the statute-book in its effects upon the interests of the farmers of the Northwest, really comes before us for discussion. Now, as to amendments to the Bill, I would first draw attention to a complaint which is made in Manitoba owing to the fact that under the present law interior elevators, that is the elevator at Winnipeg and the elva-tor at Emerson, are permitted to mix the different grades of wheat for the purpose of raising the standard of the wheat they happen to have on hand. Under the old law, as I understand it, mixing was permitted at Fort William, but the law was amended in 1890 so as to permit mixing at Emerson and Winnipeg. It is claimed by many engaged in the grain business that this results detrimentally to the quality and grade of the wheat that is being exported, as it permits those engaged in that business to use scoured wheat in 'the mixing, and pass it off for a higher grade. This is said to be a disadvantage to those from whom the wheat is bought. I have some correspondence here with regard to the matter, which 1 shall probably lay before the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright), as I see that under this Act the administration of the law is put in charge of his department-and I may say in passing, that I am pleased with that change. There is another question with regard to what are known as the small warehouses. It is claimed that men who wish to nave these small warehouses are practically debarred from doing so by that provision of the law which compels them to keep these warehouses open and keep men to look after them. Owing to the small quantity of grain that can be put through these warehouses, the expense is prohibitory.

If the bon. gentleman will permit me, I would like to ask him a question. I suppose that what he refers to as ' small warehouses ' are what are termed ' flat warehouses ' in the Bill ?
This has been the experience in the pasit regarding those warehouses. It has been claimed that while the amended Act of 1890 permitted those warehouses, it was impossible to use them, owing to the fact that they could not be made profitable.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
Does my hon. friend mean that the Act pre-Mr. BOYD.
vents the buyer from owning flat warehouses and storing his own grain ? The Act requires that flat warehouses should only be used for storing purposes.

The objection is that a man who owns one of those small flat warehouses is compelled to keep a man there to operate it, and that it is impossible for him to make it profitable. Another amendment I propose to move is that the price of wheat at Fort William should be posted once or twice a day at the stations where there is an agent and where the grain is shipped. In that way the public is made aware of the jn-ice of grain in Fort William. I may say for the benefit of the minister that in the state of Dakota and part of Minnesota a rule such as this, I understand, has been in existence for some years, and has given great satisfaction, namely, that the price of wheat at Fort William, the grades of wheat as under this Act, is telegraphed once or twice a day over the lines and posted on the blackboards or in some conspicuous place In the stations along the line.
There is another matter I will mention. It has been suggested to me by people who are deeply interested in regard to this Act, that sub-inspectors should be appointed throughout Manitoba and the territories at the large shipping points. It is claimed that men could be found who would be capable and qualified to inspect wheat at shipping points. Of course their inspection would be subject to revision at Fort William or Winnipeg if that was thought proper. But many do not approve of having their wheat subject to inspection at Winnipeg, in view of the enormous amount of wheat that has to be inspected at Winnipeg. Now, Mr. Chairman, I am going to read a letter from a gentleman who may perhaps be considered as opposed to the present Act, and as one of the agitators. I want to place it on ' Hansard ' so that the Minister of Trade and Commerce may be able at any time to refer to it. It is rather lengthy, and it may be tiresome to some hon. gentlemen who are not interested in the matter, but I think it important that it should be published so that the minister may be able to refer to it. The gentleman who writes this letter is not known to me, the letter is addressed to myself :
Winnipeg, April 9, 1902.
N. Boyd, Esq., M.P.,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-At a meeting some time ago of the Winnipeg Griin and Produce Exchange, a resolution1 was pased asking the Dominion parliament to change the Inspection Act so as to do away with the dual inspection at Fort William and make Winnipeg inspection final.
Such an action would be very injurious to the quality of Manitoba gram and would make it in worse repute than it is at the present time and every one knows it is bad enough nowr, to prove this all I have to do is to quote an interview one of the newspaper reporters had with Mr. G. R. Crowe, manager of the Northern Elevator Company, in which he said, ' Mani-

toba No. 1 Northern is selling at three cents per bushel lower than Duluth No. 1 Northern in New York.' What Mr. Crowe said was true, but why should it be when the requirements as to weight, quality, &c., are the same tor Manitoba No. 1 Northern as for Duluth No. 1 Northern ? The reason for the difference is that ' Ybe Manitoba Inspection Act ' has been formed and manipulated to suit the tastes of the monopolistic elevator companies who own the mixing elevators and whose members have ruled the grain exchange and consequently had resolutions passed which the government acted on, and the outcome is that the quality of our graded wheat has deteriorated to such an ex. tent that it will not command the aanre price that Duluth wheat of the same grade will in the worlds markets, the reason of the deterioration is that the most vicious and illegal mixing of scoured, dried and low grade wheat has taken place in the h'gh grades by the interior mixing elevators, and the Act (which was framed at the dictates of Mr. C. N. Bell, secretary of the Winnipeg Grain and Produce Exchange), practically ties the hands of the inspectors so that they cannot stop it. True, the Act gives the inspectors instructions re mixing elevators but gives them no protection in any way when appeals are made to the Survey Board, the duty of the Survey Board is to grade wheat according to the Act, and if the inspector has lowered the grade out of the mixing elevators on account of it not being- up to the average, lie loses every time. Manitoba wheat should command a premium over Duluth wheat instead of selling at three cents lower, The reason for this is that Manitoba No. 1 Northern is comprised of practically all Red Fyfe ' wheat while Duluth No. 1 Northern contains a great deal of ' Blue Stem' ' wheat, Red Fyfe ' is a much stronger and better wheat than * Blue Stem.'
About three years ago the Grain Exchange passed a resolution asking the Dominion parliament to stop the mixing of Manitoba wheat and also asking that the inspection be done at Winnipeg with inspectors at Fort William to check and correct mistakes. In June, 1899, I attended a meeting of the agricultural committee in reference to the Inspection Act, and at that meeting the present Inspection Act was keenly opposed by the following .-Messrs'. McFee, Me* Bean & Quintal, of . Montreal ; Cummings, of Lyn; Richardson, of Kingston; Meldrum of Peterboro, Flavelle, of Lindsay; Kemp, McLaughlin, Spink & Watts, of Toronto, and Bailey of Hamilton, all protested against having the inspection done at Winnipeg which was over 400 miles from Fort William (the storage point) and all demanded that if the mixing was stopped at Fort William, &c., that It should also be stopped in the interior mixing elevators at Winnipeg and Emerson. Mr. C. N. Bell demanded that the interior mixing he allowed and stated that he was acting under -instructions from the Winnipeg Grain Exchange, the Dominion parliament shut their ears to all but Mr. Bell, shut their eyes as to what would be in the best interests of the Manitoba agriculturists and at the dictation of Mr. Bell (not on the resolution of the Grain Exchange which asked that al! mixing be stopped) had the present obnoxious Inspection Act passed. After returning home, the president of the Winnipeg Grain and Produce Exchange told me that Mr. C. N. Bell's instructions were to have the mixing stopped everywhere and that he had no instructions whatever to ask to have it allowed at interior mixing elevators, this proves that Mr. Bell was wrong when he sa'd he was acting for the
Grain Exchange, instead of acting according to the Grain Exchanges instructions he acted the very opposite and his fighting for the mixing at Winnipeg and Emerson proves that he was working in the interests of the elevator monopolists.
The present Inspection Act has been in effect for over two years and a half and has proven itself to be very injurious to the farmers. It lias allowed the elevator monopolists to illegally and viciously mix and ruin the quality of graded wheat and thus allows the elevator owners to buy at under value (they have done so to an unreasonable extent for several months past).	.
We need a change in the Inspection Act, but not in the way the Grain Exchange ask. Who ever heard of any civilized country allowing wheat to be graded at over 400 miles from the storage point, yet this is what has been done in Winnipeg for over two years, any one who knows anything about wheat knows that the condition of- wheat often changes while a car is going less than 100 miles, during the month of September a great many farmers thresh direct from the stock and load at once into cars, as wheat does not sweat in the stook. I have several times seen cars pass Winnipeg in which the wheat was sweating and which the inspector graded ' tough,' but which on its arrival at Fort William was past the sweating stage and quite dry, consequently graded straight. Again during hot weather in summer I have seen wheat which was in good condition and graded straight in . Winnipeg arrive in Fort William very much heated and the inspector refused to grade it straight. This proves the inspection should be done at Fort William instead of at Winnipeg.
The Canadian Pacific Railway refuse to hold cars in Winnipeg so that they can be sampled in daylight, and in some cases a train will come in and leave again in such a short time that the samplers have not time to thoroughly examine the cars they are sampling, as every one knows not even the most expert grain-man can tell the grade of wheat by lamplight, so how can the samplers tell whether the cars are plugged with low grade wheat or not when they are forced to rush through and sample at night. Under the Old Inspection Act all cars were held on txack at Fort William for daylight sampling so that the samplers could find almost without exception all ears that were plugged and the inspector punished the dishonest shipper by lowering the grade down to the poorest quality that could be found in the car. Under the preseift Inspection Act plugged cars cannot help but pass the samplers very often as they are. forced to sample at night. The consequence of this is to further lower the quality of our wheat and again proves the inspection should be done at Fort William intead of at Winnipeg.
Another proof and the most forcible one is that I have known of a lot of cases where the inspector at Fort William refused to allow the cars to he unloaded at Fort William on the inspection certificate that had been issued at Winnipeg and the inspector at Winnipeg was forced to ask for the return of the certificate and replace it with a new one, sometimes the grtide was raised but very often it was lowered. Tnis again proves that Winnipeg is not the right place at which to inspect grain but that it should be inspected at Fort William.
In face of all the rankness of the Inspection Act, the Grain Exchange or rather the elevator monopolists who rule the exchange and use'it as a blind, again have the nerve to ask the Dominion parliament to change the Act and make

by the dealers at Carberry or at Winnipeg. In the case of these three cars which seemed a very peculiar thing, all of the dealers concluded that one particular car would go No. 1 hard and that the other two cars would go No. 1 Northern, but strange to say the car that they supposed would go No. 1 hard, went No. 1 Northern, and the other two cars went No. 1 hard. When the return came back from Winnipeg the grainmen said : There you see our position ; it is impossible for us to inspect this wheat for the reasons that when we decide on what we think is No. 1 hard we invariably get upset by the inspector in Winnipeg. That is one of the reasons why I think that we should have sub-inspectors at those larger interior points. I think a sub-inspector could inspect at a point where there would be 100,000 bushels of wheat or 200,000 bushels, and that he could pass along to one or two other stations and do the inspecting there. That would stop a great deal of this scheming and sharp practice that lias been perpetrated for some time past. I shall give another practical instance of what has occurred this last season. Take the town of Douglas, where there was a Mr. Greenwood, who is outside of the present grain exchange, buying wheat. On a certain day there was a difference of 10 cents a bushel on wheat, paid by the same firm at the town of Douglas and at the town of Sydney, which is 40 or 50 miles nearer the market. At Sydney the firm that was there opposing Mr. Greenwood was paying 10 cents less per bushel for wheat for the same grade of No. 1 Northern than they were paying at Douglas. There is something wrong when people can be treated like that. I am not here for the purpose of trying to gain the slightest political advantage in this matter. I am simply here to offer suggestions which I believe will enable the government at the present time, or as soon as possible to make that Grain Act as perfect as it can be made. There is another matter which I would like to mention with regard to this question and it is this : In the existing Act there is a certain dockage allowed. Those who buy wheat seem to have the privilege under the present Act, of taxing the wheat to a certain extent.
I will give an experience that I myself had. I shipped one car of wheat to Fort William and had something over 600 bushels of wheat in it. The dockage by the government weigher was, I think, 46 pounds; that is about three quarters of one bushel.
I sold 800 bushels of wheat to a merchant in Carberry and he took out 32 bushels, or 4 bushels to the hundred weight, and this was the same wheat. Well, if he had given back the dockage it would not have amounted to so much, but he gave back only 14 bushels and kept 18. I said:	If you take
this wheat out, you should give it back. He said:	No, under the Act, we keep it for
dockage. If they take anything from you in the way of dockage, they should give it
back to you. If you take any other produce to market, such as cheese or butter, and there is anything wrong with it which results in them taking dockage, they do not keep a certain amount from you. I do not think it was the intention of the framers of this Act that this should take place, and I propose to move an amendment in regard to it. I think I have said sufficient at present to show the way I feel in regard to it. I believe that if cars were given to the farmers, and if loading platforms were erected, the trouble would be overcome, because those engaged in the grain business would understand that they cannot force us to pass our grain through their elevators, and that while we are prepared to do business with them as long as they act fairly, if they do not treat us properly we can ship our own grain by our own cars. I see in the Act these words: ' without undue delay.' It is not my wish to be harsh or unfair with the railway companies, but I would like some of the lawyers in the House to tell me exactly what those words mean. I suppose they would mean a reasonable time, and if so, I am not going to raise any very serious objection.

Mr. Chairman, I very much regret that this Bill was not placed in the hands of hon. gentlemen earlier. I may say that I placed it before the House as soon as I, myself, was fully in possession of the amendments which I have been led to believe were desired by a large majority of the members of this House who are more intimately acquainted with this matter than I myself am. I would suggest to the hon. member (Mr. Boyd), that, if I followed him correctly, a great many of the remarks that he has just made, and in particular the letter which he has just read to the committee, do not apply to the Manitoba Grain Act. hut to the Inspection Act. Am I correct in that ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I do not know.
We are now dealing with the question of amendments of the Grain Act, and I think a great deal of what he said refers to the Inspection Act, which is a different Act. Is that not so ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I do not so understand it. It may be possible in regard to the letter, but, perhaps the writer is finding fault with both Acts.

It is more particularly the Inspection Act of which he complains, whicli is a separate Act, and which we are not proposing to deal with in this Bill at all. Of course, I am aware that in bringing down anything of this kind at this stage of the session it is practically impossible to consider more than is now before us with any degree of profit. An immense number

of suggestions may be made, many of them very proper and very desirable, but ones that we can hardly consider now. I would suggest to the hon. gentleman that we take up each particular amendment that is proposed, and if the committee considers that that particular amendment is likely to be useful, we can pass that and I will take careful note of what my hon. friends on either side of the House suggest as to future improvements, but I would be rather chary about making any material alterations in the Act without due consideration. Of course, the Grain Inspection Act and Grain Act have only been very recently put under the charge of the Department of Trade and Commerce, and I have not yet been able to acquaint myself as well as I could wish with the practical working of these Acts. We have a commissioner engaged in dealing with these questions. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Boyd) himself knows that the circumstances which occurred last autumn were very exceptional. There was not only a vastly larger crop than ever before, but owing to certain climatic conditions, I believe that the time for moving the crop was very much shortened. I think I am correct in saying that there was scarcely more than half the time to handle double the crop, and I think under those circumstances there was much greater difficulty on the part of the railway company in meeting the demands of the inhabitants than would have occurred under ordinary conditions. Rut. I think lion, gentlemen will agree with me that the best we can do at present is to consider each one of these amendments that is proposed on its merits and by itself. I. myself, have a perfectly open mind. All I desire is, as far as we can, to improve the Act for the benefit of all concerned, and I can assure the hon. gentleman and all other hon. gentlemen who are specially concerned in the matter that I will take very careful note of any suggestions that they may have to offer. I am not in a position to say that I can accept at an hour's notice important amendments even if they appear to me to be very desirable. These things require to be very carefully considered before we can put them on the statute-book, but I will lie glad if we should confine ourselves, as much as may be, to the particular subject of the Grain Act, leaving the Inspection Act to be considered hereafter, and if we should confine ourselves to the special questions which are brought up in the amendments which I have now the honour of submitting to the committee.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.
