speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
As the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce has said, he is put in the position of having to consider a subject which until lately was in charge of the Department of Inland Revenue, and it is, as hon. gentlemen from the North-west Territories will all agree, almost impossible for a person who is not personally acquainted with the conditions of the grain trade to familiarize himself with the complicated working of the Inspection Act and ttlie Grain Adt. In fact, it is difficult to get two persons who are well acquainted with the workings of the grain trade to agree to what the law should be. There are two Acts which cover the transaction of the business-the Inspection Act and the Groin Act. The functions of the two Acts are very different. The Inspection Act provides the way in which the grades of wheat shall be fixed. The Grain Act consists of a series of regulations affecting the handling of the wheat by the buyer and the seller ; the storage of the wheat; the conduct of warehousemen, and a variety of regulations for the purpose of protecting the producers and enabling them to get the fair value of their grain. Hon. members who were hero in 1899, when the Inspection Act was revised, will remember that it was referred to a special committee, and mo piece of legislation which has been passed by this House since I have been a member of it, received more thorough and more anxious consideration in every clause and every line .than that Act. Sir Henry Joly was then Minister of Inland Revenue, and besides having the departmental duty of looking specially after the matter, ho took ia very warm personal interest in it. He attended the sittings of the committee; nearly all the North-west members also attended; persons interested in the matter on both sides, men in favour of independent buying, persons representing the farming interest, the millers, and', the grain dealers, were all at different times before the committee; and every provision in that Bill was worked out with as great care as any committee of this House is capable of giving to any Bill. I do not mean by that to suggest that the Bill is perfect-far from it; but I venture to say that it has worked as well as could possibly be expected, after all the difficult and changing circumstances which it has had to meet.
There are two special matters to which my hon. friend lias referred, which require

a moment's attention at least. One Is the objection which I have not heard to-day for ; the first time. I presume it has come to ' my hon. friend in the same way that it has come to me. It is that in elevators that are known in the North-west-not as public elevators, but storing elevators, there is an amount of mixing done which is detrimental to the reputation of the North-west wheat. That, I understand, is the objection of my hon. friend. Am I correct ?
Yes.

The gerieral principle of the Inspection Act is that a man in his own elevator In the interior of the country may mix as he likes, but that when he puts his wheat into what is called the terminal or public elevator, it is graded, and it cannot be mixed, nor can the grading be deteriorated by any mixing that takes place after it passes into the hands of the inspector. It was suggested at the time the Act was passed, that possibly there might be elevators used for storing purposes in the interior of the country, and that in these storing elevators, where the wheat does not pass through the hands of an inspector, and therefore is not graded at all in the sense understood in the inspection Act, that might possibly take place which my bon. friend and other people say to some extent does take place. I have heard, as my hon. friend has, that it does take place, and section 13 of the Inspection Act of 1899 was adopted for the purpose of correcting that. If what my hon. -friend states and what 1 have heard from other quarters is true, it simply means that this clause has not .been acted upon.
I cannot myself imagine any method which the hon. gentleman could now suggest which would be any more effective than this clause. If you are going to provide a remedy by legislation, you must put it into the hands of somebody to decide whether the complaint is founded on fact or not; because it is a question of fact. You have the right under the Act to bring the matter to the attention of the inspector, and lie is required to make an, investigation; and if he does not do so in a satisfactory manner. you can take the complaint before the minister himself, and have it fairly and fully investigated. I do not think the committee which had this subject under consideration could have devised any better plan than the plan provided in the Act; and if that weapon is not being employed, I think the fault lies with those who have knowledge of .the fact, and who do not take the necessary steps to remedy the evil complained of. I may say, 'however, that in as much as the matter is now drawn to the attention of the minister, the facts might justify him in having a careful examination made as to whether the elevator in Winnipeg has been guilty of the violation of the principle of the Act.
Then, my .hon. friend referred to a desire on the part of some people that there should
be a change in the system of inspection so as to provide for the appointment of subinspectors throughout the country, instead of allowing the inspection to take place in Winnipeg, by having all the wheat pass through the hands of the chief inspector. That subject was also Considered in 1899 at the time the Act was passed, and a good many statements and opinions in regard to it have been brought before me from time to time; but 1 am bound to say that up to tlie present time I have never known a ease to be made out showing that the producer would derive any special benefit from a change in the system.
I do not say that he would not, but I cannot declare imyself positively as convinced either one way or the other. There has not been any sufficiently strong case made out to convince me that any substantial benefit would result from such a change. At present the wheat goes to the yard. A sample is taken from the car to the office of the chief inspector, and by that sample the grade is determined. My hon. friend refers to a case in which, when the dealers shipped the wheat, it went as one grade, and When the farmer shipped it, it went as a lower grade. I do not know how this particular fact is established, but I do not think that there has been any deliberate fraud on the part of the chief inspector. If there 'be a suggestion of any fraud or dishonesty on his .part, it would be the immediate duty of the government to take every possible means of having a most thorough investigation. I have never, during the time I have to do with the question, in one way or another, heard the slightest suggestion made by any one that there was any doubt whatever of the complete integrity of the chief Inspector, Mr. Horne. I have not the (honour of his personal acquaintance, but have never heard any but the highest opinions expressed regarding him, and I have not the slightest doubt that his integrity is above suspicion. It is possible, however, that in the handling of a thousand cars of wheat, a number of 'the cars might be transposed by mistake and mixed up together, but that would not be the only possible way in which I think such a mistake could occur, as to have wheat of the same quality shipped by two different parties graded differently.
I think that on the whole my hon. friend will agree that, considering all the difficulties attending the inspection of wheat, there is not very much fault to find with the result of the inspection system. But the result of the inspection system and the result of the shipping system, are two dif-i fereut things altogether. My hon. friend ! says that at Douglas last year, where there was an independent buyer, he was aide to pay 10 cents a bushel more than did the buyers who represented the elevator people. I have heard a similar statement made with regard to other places, and I am free to say that the facts show distinctly that there was a most remarkable difference in

the prices, to say the least, which were ottered those representing the elevator owners and the independent 'buyers who have no connection with that combine.
The amendments which my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce is proposing, are Intended to meet that ditticulty. If I have any understanding at all of the difficulty, it consists of two main things. First, there is the shortage of ears, and legislation of this character will not increase the supply of cars, tout we have succeeded in another way in making it certain that there will be a very largely augmented supply during next year. A very large sum -is being devoted by the Canadian Pacific Railway to the procuring of rolling stock for their operations during next year, and we may look with some degree of confidence to a great deal of relief in that respect. Rut the position of the farmers, which we are trying to remedy by this Bill, is this. The disadvantage under which tlhe farmer suffered was that the elevator people knew that the farmer was not in a position to handle ills grain except through them. The shortage of cars largely prevented the farmers from being able to ship independently. That wns the result of a combination of circumstances. It is alleged that the wheat buyer would not pay wliat the wheat was worth. The wliea-t buyers, of course, do not admit this, and it is not necessary for us to say wihat we think about it. But we all deplore the fact that, for a considerable portion of the season a.t least, the men who raised the wheat did not get its full value, and what we are really trying to do in -this Bill ,is to put the farmer in as independent a position as possible, so far as the wiiea-t -buyer is concerned. We give him the right to put up -a flat warehouse if he chooses, and a loaded platform, or to ship from the track, aud make -the company furnish him with cars if he wants them. That is about all that tills House, with the information it has, can dio to put the farmers in a position to soy to the grain buyers : We are independent and we can deal with you on equal terms; if you will not give us tlhe full value of the wheat, we will deal with -it ourselves. If my hon. friend w-ill look through the amendments, be will find tliat they are carefully drawn for the purpose iof bringing about that result.
In so far as the suggestions respecting the amendments to the Inspection Act are concerned, every member of the committee will agree that a radical change in the, system of inspecting wheat could not he -made in any other way than by bringing in a measure at the very beginning of the session, getting -the very best committee that co-ulil be appointed to deal with it, and g-iving the matter the most careful and protracted consideration.
I am quite confident-that as we go through the clauses, it will be seen that they have been carefully drawn- for the purpose of bringing about the results we all have in

view. There was a suggestion made by my hon. friend respecting the posting of the prices of wheat. I do not know that any objection can be| raised to that. I do not know to what extent it would be an advantage. I-t might in many ways be an advantage to the farmers to know wliat wheat was worth at Fort William; and if that suggestion would -work to the advantage to the producer of wheat, I see no reason why it should not be adopted.

Who is to pay the expense of getting -the quotations and posting -them two or three times a week ail over the territories ? It will be quite a heavy expense to get those telegrams from all the stations along the different lines of railway, and I do not think it is necessary. The farmers get the daily papers and mail and know pretty well the prices of grain in Winnipeg, and why should we put the dealers to the heavy expense of getting those telegrams and posting them up ?
Do not the local dealers already every day have the prices -telegraphed them by their head firms, and could they not be compelled to have them posted up publicly ?

At some of the principal points, n-o doubt they do, but I do not suppose that in all the points they get those telegrams daily. I do not see how you could force the dealers to put up information which they get for their own private use.

It strikes me that, if the assertion is true, t-hat a difference of as much as 10 cents a bushel in the price of wheat exists between stations where there is competition and stations where there is no competition, then, in the interest of the great public of the North-west Territories, in the interest of the men who have gone into that country to indure its hardships and open it up to industry, the government would be quite justified in incurring whatever expense is necessary to carry out a plan that would afford them protection. And it seems to me that the suggestion that at all the stations where wheat is bought the prices ruling at Winnipeg shall be posted is one that is in the public interest. It might not serve the interest of buyers who wish to buy wheat 10 cents cheaper at one station than at another, but it would be in the interest of the farmer. We are trying to induce settlers to go into the country, and the men who go there at our instance are, in a sense, our wards, and we are their guardians. If these men are liable to be made a prey of by monopolists, and if giving them information will enable them to judge whether they are being dealt fairly with or not and whether they are receiving day by day the prices they ought to receive. I think that information ought to be afforded 1 them.

In reply to some of tlie remarks of the Minister of the Interior, L may say that, as is known to lion, members, I was not in the House when these Acts were passed. Before I returned, the present Grain Act and the Inspection Act so far as it relates to grain, were passed. If, as has been stated by the Minister of the Interior, I have confused the two Acts or misunderstood them, it is a misunderstanding or confusion that prevails generally among the farmers throughout the country. This is one of the reasons that makes it all the more unfortunate that this Bill should be brought before us so late in the session. Had it been brought forward earlier, we could have proposed such amendments to the Inspection Act as would have removed the disability under which we labour. My hon. friend from West York seems to feel keenly the question of expense, and asks who is to pay for procuring and disseminating the information as to the prices of wheat. I think the hon. gentleman need not worry; for, if the fees now charged under the Inspection Act are not sufBcient for this purpose, a few cents added to these fees will fully cover the outlay, and the farmers, upon whom the burden will rest, will not object to the additional expense for such a purpose. The information will enable us to show these people what they are actually taking out of the farmers. If we know what the different grades of wheat are bringing at Fort William, and the freight, it is easy to know what price the grain men can afford to pay.

I would suggest that it would be better to take up each clause in turn and not go into a general discussion at this stage of the session, of the Inspection Act, with which the Grain Act has nothing at all to do. I have taken careful note of the hon. gentleman's suggestion as to telegraphing the prices of wheat and would like to make some further inquiry about it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: As my hon. friend (Mr. Boyd) will admit, the only way in which that could be worked out would be by a section requiring the railway station agent to post up the prices.

I may say that we have an arrangement under which daily reports from the three fishing stations in the three maritime provinces are received daily and are imblished in Halifax at the expense of
the government. Something to the same effect might be done in this instance.

I would suggest that, following the ordinary rules of the Committee of the Whole, we should taxe up one clause and consider it. We shall make no progress if we traverse the whole Grain Act and Inspection Act. But there will be every opportunity to consider amendments if we take up one section at a time.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. Boyd) was merely giving the Minister of Trade and Commerce notice of what was to come.
On section 2,	'
1 wish to move an amendment to this by inserting the word ' first ' after the word ' six,' making it read ' the six first standard grades of wheat.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Referring for a moment to the first section of the Act, it seems to be an unusual mode of legislation to say that the expression ' Minister of Inland Revenue ' should mean ' Minister of Trade and Commerce.' I do not see the object of it.
In the Manitoba Grain Act the Minister of Inland Revenue had charge of this matter, and within a few months it has been transferred by special statute to the Department of Trade and Commerce.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I would like to suggest another amendment. The Agricultural Committee of the Manitoba legislature had an investigation into this Act at the last session of parliament and were going to memorialize this parliament in reference to certain amendments. But unfortunately those amendments were brought down on the last day of the session and they were talked out, and I presume the memorial never reached the government. One of the proposed amendments was to subsection 3, to make it more definite. It was to insert after the word ' forward ' in the second line thereof, the words ' to tlie order of the owner thereof when requested to do so by him.' Also to strike out the words * without delay ' from the fourteenth line of the same subsection and to substitute therefor the words ' within twenty-four hours.' ' Without delay ' seemed to them a rather indefinite term.

I am sorry that this matter was delayed to the present time. If the hon. gentleman will write out his amendments and forward them to me I will have them examined. But I am rather reluctant, unless for very strong cause, and because it would probably imperil the passage of the Bill to embark on a discussion of more than the amendments that are now suggested. If the hon. gentleman thinks that the proposals

that are made are to the general advantage I would suggest to him that it would be better to confine ourselves to these than to run the risk of losing them all. We all know that there is considerable risk in taking up absolutely new questions and inserting them in sections which are not now before us without an opportunity to compare them with the other portions oif the Bill. I do not say that his suggestions are not all right, but I would like to have a little time to consider them.
On section 3,
The MINISTER OF TRADE ANI) COMMERCE. I explained to the committee that the changes proposed to be made are chiefly these : At present ten farmers are required to apply, the present amendment reduces the ten to one. It strikes out the last clause which provides that in the case of each additional warehouse the applicants desirous of erecting it should be liable to pay rental of 6 per cent interest on the value of the land taken, such land to be determined and fixed by commissioners, and should be .liable to pay the cost of constructing the necessary sidings. That portion is struck out. Now I observe that an addition has been made here. In the original clause of the Act of 1900 a flat warehouse covered with metal is provided. The words ' covered with metal ' are omitted. Those words I think ought to be inserted again, and I move that they be inserted.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I would like to remark that in the Bill of 1900 the erection of a flat wareSiouse utas surrounded) with so many restrictions that it was found that people were not ready to build them. It was thought better simply to state that they might build a flat warehouse and that all those details in connection with it should be left to the discretion of the warehouse commissioner; that it was quite unnecessary to define what the building should be, inasmuch as it was largely in the hands of the warehouse commissioner and the railway committee. I do not suppose that at this date and age they would think of anything else but a metal roof, even in view of the insurance. We considered it was not necessary to enter into any minute description of the building.
Strong objection was taken to the omission of those words, and I think the objection was well taken.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I have no objection to their being replaced, I do not suppose it matters much.

The railway companies object very strongly to the omission of the words ,
' covered with metal ' on the ground that it | affects the insurance on everything surrounding.	I
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I would point out that the railway companies do not cover with metal all the buildings which they place on then-own property. It is perfectly true that in most cases, where these flat warehouses are erected in proximity to other buildings, it would be no doubt wise to have a provision in the Act that they should be covered with metal, but I think this may be safely left in the hands of the commissioner. There will doubtless be cases where warehouses will be located hundreds of yards away from any other building, and in such cases it would not be necessary to enforce the provision that the buildings should be covered with metal. I think it may be safely left to the discretion of the commissioner.

I sympathize to some extent with what my hon. friend (Mr. Scott) says, but it must be remembered that we are practically letting down the bars and giving the greatest possible facility for the construction of flat warehouses. We are not providing in this Bill that a flat warehouse shall be of any particular capacity. A warehouse mav only have a capacity of L000 bushels. Even if a warehouse should be put up 300 or 000 feet away from another elevator, next day a man might come along and apply for a site near the same place for the erection of an elevator that will cost $10,000 or $15,000. If you have two or three little flat warehouses, frame, and not covered with metal, you raise a difficulty at once. You raise a dispute, you have reference to the commissioner and there is a question as to whether this man shall be compelled to cover Ills warehouse with metal or not. It seems to me that the simplest way is to provide that the flat warehouse must be covered with metal, and there will toe no difficulty about it. If it were going to cost sufficient to impose any restriction on the erection of flat warehouses I would not suggest it. but it is a trifling matter in the case of a small warehouse. and it is well understood to be in the general interest that it should be done.

I do not see any objection to that provision and I believe that on the whole it possibly will be in the interest of the farmers that a flat warehouse should be so covered as it affects the rate of insurance and other matters. I would like to have the hon. minister's interpretation of the Act as to this question : Must a man who owns one of these small warehouses keep it open for the use of the public ?

I am not very familiar with the working of the Act, but if my hon. friend (Sir Richard Cartwright) will look at subsections 4, 5 and 6 of section 41, he will see that it rather looks as if the owner will require to keep his warehouse open.
I do not see anything making it absolutely imperative in tjiis clause.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: No, it does not say so in so many words.
And I think if the hon. gentleman will look at section 8 he will see that we are removing a restriction on the buying and selling of grain which will probably obviate any practical difficulty.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: ' That, of course, permits the use of it for his own grain, but is not the effect bf subsections 4, 5, 6, that he must keep it open for business by other persons ? I do not know whether it Is the best policy that he should be obliged to keep it open or not ; I am not speaking of the question of policy but merely as to the effect of this section.
On the question of construction. That, of course, is more a legal question, but, reading it cursorily, I should hardly think that he could be compelled to keep a man there all the time.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
Subsection 4 of section 41 of the Act says :
The owner of any such warehouse shall on the application of any farmer undertaking to ship a car load of grain, allot such farmer a binn in such warehouse as soon as one is available.
He is bound to permit his warehouse to be used for the purpose of shipping, but there is nothing in the Act that compels him to keep a man there. It is an obligation which could not be placed upon anybody by implication. It would have to be clear and specific.
I should think that is right, but if the farmer goes to him at his house he will be obliged to go down to the warehouse and allow him to put his grain in.
The elevator man will have to take the consequences.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: The elevator man will have to go and open up his warehouse and let the farmer put his grain in, because the statute says so.

I remember that when the first Act was passed the commissioner reported upon the question, and after investigating it he was imbued with the idea that the warehouse should not be used by a buyer ; that is to say, that the owner Should not buy wheat himself and therefore the principle was embodied in the Act that flat warehouses should simply be a means of shipping, but the experience of the community there is against It. They seem to require that you should allow a small independent buyer to have a flat warehouse to buy grain and increase the competition on the market.

I take it that practically these
warehouses would not be in use for more than two months or thereabouts. Would not that be the practical result ? It is in the autumn when the grain is threshed and prior to the close of navigation that these things will be of real use to the farmers. As matters now stand I think by removing the restrictions on the purchase and sale of grain we will make it very much to the interest of the proprietor of the flat warehouse to be anxious to receive anything he can get.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I know that it was frequently said by those interested in building these small warehouses that that was one of the reasons why they did not take advantage of the Act.

The objection was, that, not being able to buy grain, they could not get the profit of buying. They could only make a storage charge for the wheat which they received and the small quantity which a flat warehouse held did not pay. But now, the owner is enabled to make a profit by buying grain and I do not think there is any difficulty about that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I am prepared to let it pass on the strength of the legal interpretation we have had and to take our chance of the future interpretation of the court if necessity demands it.

There is a suggestion which I would like to make. I see by this Act that you are confined to building nothing but a flat warehouse. I do not see why there should not be a provision which would enable a person to build either a flat warehouse, or an elevator. Last year we wanted to build an elevator in place of a flat warehouse, and we found a provision in the law under which we could build a flat warehouse, but there was no provision for us to build an elevator, and we could not get the right of way from the company. I-t is in the interest of the country that elevators should be built in place of flat warehouses, and I do not see why we should not have the privilege of building them. If the farmers have enough money to build an elevator they ought to be allowed to build it.
Is tue expression ' flat warehouse ' defined by statute or is it merely a term known to the trade.
So far as I am aware it is not defined by statute.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: There does not seem to be any restriction on the height of a flat warehouse.
An elevator is a warehouse, but a warehouse is not necessarily an elevator. An elevator is a warehouse which has machinery for lifting the grain.

I understand that, but there does not seem to be any restriction in this statute on making a flat warehouse as high as one likes, and there is nothing in the Act to prevent you from having machinery in it. Why does it not authorize the building of an elevator ?
I do not say that it does not, but these are questions which are often required to be determined by the court.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: 1 want to have the word ' elevator ' inserted because we do not want to have any trouble about it. We got a lawyer last year and he advised us that we could not build an elevator under the provisions of the Act.
1 am not disputing that. I was merely seeking information from the minister as to the meaning of the statute.

I took the expression ' flat warehouse ' as I found it in the Manitoba Grain Act of 1900. I am willing to consider all these amendments together.

speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I would like to have a legal interpretation of the meaning of the words ' undue delay,' in the clause requiring railway companies to furnish cars to farmers without undue delay. Do they mean forty-eight hours, a week, or how long ?

I think I can answer that question by asking my hon. friend to try to express the idea better. I think he would then realize the difficulty of trying to regulate business by an Act of parliament. The only thing we can do is to employ general terms which are to be understood in their ordinary and common sense. You cannot say in an Act of parliament that if a man asks a railway company for a car for a certain purpose the company shall furnish it to him within a certain time, because unforeseen circumstances might render it impossible to do so. I think my hon. friend will see that we have gone just as far as we could go in a legislative enactment by declaring what the duty of the company shall be. Undue delay means unreasonable delay. If you covered pages of the statute-book with explanations I do not believe you could make the provision any more effective.
The real difficulty is this. The railway companies bring a certain number of cars to every shipping point, and what we want to provide is that the farmers shall get a fair proportion of these cars.

This particular clause has no reference to the distribution of cars so much as it is to make provision that the cars shall be furnished to farmers at all points-not only where there are loading platforms, but at other points.

This clause lays down the principle that the farmer is entitled to get his share of cars. The company canfaot say, ' we are only bound to furnish cars where there is a warehouse or an elevator.' We settled that question by this clause.

I have no desire to hamper the railway companies in doing business. But the minister has asked me if I would

suggest something that would be more effective. I could very soon do it, but it is a question whether it would be exactly fair to the railway companies. For instance, if a farmer keeps a car for a certain time and does not load it he has to pay for the car. If, ou the other hand, you provide that when the farmer demands a car within a certain time the company shall pay if they do not furnish it within that time, you wiil get over the difficulty. But for my part,
1	suppose we may be satisfied in the meantime to see how the railway companies are prepared to meet the provisions of the Act so far as we have gone and deal with them later on if they do not do so.
I think that would be the wiser course. This Act will, I think, be up for revision next year, and in the meantime we shall have an opportunity of seeing how it will work.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

I think that should be left in the hands of the commissioner who is on the ground and knows the conditions. There are places where there is plenty of grain, but where there is not a siding for a distance of twenty miles.

I move the addition to section
2	of the words ' and where there is no station yard at such siding as the commissioner may prescribe.'

On section 8,

I beg to submit the following amendment: On the second line between the words ' agent ' and ' and ' that the following words be inserted. ' Tnere shall be a suitable blackboard, upon which the prices of all grains offered for sale under this Act shall be plainly written daily at 9 a.m. and 1 p.m.' [DOT]
Who will do this work-the railway company or the government ?
Take it out of the inspection commission.

Provision is made in the Act to provide papers giving the prices in Liverpool and other points, and also Chicago and Minneapolis, to be seen every day in Winnipeg, so that the suggestion of the hon. member for Macdonald is simply to carry this forward from Winnipeg to outlying stations.

There are nearly a thousand such
stations, and this might be a very considerable tax on the Inspection Act, which is hardly equal to the requirements made on it, as it stands. I would like a little time to consider that amendment, and I hope, when we come to the third reading, to be able to give an answer. There is no limit to the time in the amendment, and to supply for several months prices' twice a day to a thousand stations might involve much greater i expense than the hon. gentleman contemplates. I suppose his intention is that these prices shall be supplied by the Canadian Pacific Telegraph Company, which is tne only company that has communication with all these stations. From my own experience, I should say that to supply twice a day to a thousand places by telegraph the prices of all kinds of wheat offered for sale under this Act, might involve a very considerable charge. Judging from my own experience, I should say that to supply, twice a day, telegraphic statements to a thousand places of the price of all the grades of wheat offered for sale under this Act might involve a very considerable charge. It might run into a great many thousand dollars.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: And what about the ease of places where they load from the platform ?
Of course, where there is no telegraph, it cannot be done.
Then, one portion of the community would be protected and the other not.
It is better to have some protected than none.

While it is, without doubt, important and desirable that the farmers selling wheat should know what that wheat is worth at Port Arthur afloat, as a matter of fact, the only way in which that could be brought about is by making some kind of amicable arrangement with the railway companies who have the telegraph lines, to furnish it.
That is the way the Agricultural Committee of the legislature decided to do it-to make the request of the railway companies.

Without warning, or notice, or discussion, to put a statutory obligation on the railway companies would not be so advantageous, I should think, as for the department to try to make an amicable arrangement with the companies. My impression is that there would be no great difficulty about it, but, of course, I cannot speak with certainty. But my hon. friend will see that it would be much better to make the attempt, because if the railway companies desire to do it, they have the facilities, hav-iug both the means of communication and a staff of officers to post up the informa-

tion. But, if you make it obligatory by statute, you do two tilings. In the first place, you are to a certain extent, making yourself responsible for the correctness of the prices quoted, which is not altogether a satisfactory thing to do. The hon. gentleman knows that, on the street in Winnipeg you may meet a man who will say :
I will give you so much for wheat, and five minutes after he might be willing to give you two cents more. Under such circumstances, who is to say what the price really is at Port Arthur. The only thing you can do is to give it as nearly as possible, and it will be much more satisfactory if that were done under an amicable arrangement with all parties than under a statute which, the railway companies would naturally feel, imposed upon them a duty which it was difficult to perform. 1 think it would be better for the department first to attempt to work out the' arrangement with the railway companies than to make it statutory.

For my part, I can see no difficulty about this being carried into effect. At the present time in many places in Manitoba-and for that matter, throughout Canada-we get market quotations hourly. And, as I say, if it is necessary to make a charge on the farmers, a very small charge on the millions of bushels of wheat going to Port Arthur would meet all the extra expense, and the farmers would be well remunerated by the service that would be rendered them in posting up these prices.
I quite agree with my hon. friend.

If the hon. minister agrees, there need be no great difficulty in working out the details. I have offered the suggestion and am satisfied to leave it with the minister until the third reading of the Bill. In the meantime, he can confer with his officers and devise a means of carrying out an improvement which, in my opinion, is absolutely necessary. And I think that hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House who represent the grain sellers of this country will support me.

I will accept my hon. friend's (Mr. Boyd's) suggestion. We will take this into consideration and will announce our conclusion on the third reading of the Bill. I wish to make a further amendment in this clause. It has been represented that there are a number of shipping stations in the same agency, and that it would be desirable to amend the section so as to include the various shipping points where there is no agent permanently resident. Also I propose to strike out the words ' forty-eight hours.' The first part of the section then would read :
At each station where there is a railway agent and where grain is shipped under such agent, an order book for cars shall be kept open to the
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
public for each shipping point under such agent in which applicants for cars shall make order. Applicants shall make order according to their requirements ; cars so ordered shall be awarded to applicants according to the order in time in which such orders appear on the Order book.
And s-o on.

This clause seems to me the most curious piece of legislation I ever read. I do not see how it is possible #to carry it out. Suppose a party who has ordered a car, and after a delay of 48 hours, if he does not take it, it is awarded to the next person. If the next person does not take it within 48 hours, when there are a couple of hundred applicants, it may be. bow long will it be before some one will appear who will take it ? It is impossible to work out anything of the kind.

If the individual does not appear the railway company can come upon liim for demurrage, if he does not use the car within 48 hours. Under the common Railway Act an individual has 48 hours within which to use the car, and it would be only just that the railway company should charge demurrage for the detention of the car.
.Hon. Mr. HAGGART. There is no provision for demurrage. Suppose there are fifty applicants for a car. The first man forfeits his right in 48 hours. The next man. may live five miles or ten miles from the station. Notice is to be sent to him. who is to send the notice, or who is to pay for sending it ? Even if he lives convenient to the station, he has 48 hours more to wait, and so it runs on, and the railroad company has to keep the cars there all the time. I do not see how you can make any practical use of this kind of legislation.

My hon. friend's imagination may suggest a great many difficulties which are not likely to occur in the practical working out of this clause. There will be no attempt to send a word to anybody that there is a car there waiting for him. Cars are coming in every hour of the day, and no station agent will keep a car 48 hours if the applicant is not there to take it. If a man has ordered a car and is there he will get it, if he is not there, he won't get it, and it will be given to the next man who is there. The real effect of this clause is to give an individual the right to order a car and to get a car, the railway company are compelled to furnish him a car. I am not disposed to be unreasonable with the railway company. I recognize the fact that it is a very difficult business for any station agent to handle the business at a point where there is an immense amount of wheat, and perhaps a shortage of cars. But at the same time there are substantial grievances on the part of the farmers. Every member of the House who represents a

wheat growing constituency in the Northwest will know of cases where cars have gone by day after day, where there are people at an elevator or warehouse who are entitled to cars and cannot get them. What we desire is a law which shall give to each man fair play and no discrimination. There may be practical difficulty in working out the clause, but I do not think any better way can be suggested of attaining the object we have in view. The clause has received very careful consideration.

The hon. minister says that it practically will accomplish what is required. Fancy thirty applicants where there is a forfeiture and every one waiting his turn. The station master has absolute control over the matter and if the first one forfeits his right he passes over him and goes oh with the rest.

If we have conditions in future in any way approaching what we had last year there will be no danger of forfeiture. I know of a case last year at a station ten miles north of Regina Where three or four cars were placed on a siding on Sunday night. Before daylight on Monday these cars were all filled. The farmers left home with their loads at midnight and loaded the cars.

I am not dreading very much the fear that the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Haggart) has suggested in regard to this. I desire to mention the amendment which I propose to move to clause 54 and which I will hand to the minister. It is in regard to dockage. I propose to add to section 54 the words ' and shall be given the full amount of dockage from their grain if they desire the same.' I explained that merchants who buy grain are In the habit of docking the grain very heavily and then keeping over half of it. It is to prevent this practice that I suggest the amendment.

I would remind my hon. friend (Mr. Boyd) that the legislation of the North-west Territories effectually stands in the way of this amendment. This matter was discussed at very great length in connection with the Bill with persons well acquainted with the condition of things in the west. The Noxious Weeds Act of the North-west Territories stands in the way of what may be taken as dockage being given back to the individual who owns the grain.
What are the general provisions of the Noxious Weeds Act ?
That the Individual shall not be allowed to take the stuff which has been cleaned out of his grain, put it in his conveyance and take it home, because he would scatter the weed seeds all the way.
If there are noxious weed seeds in the refuse or small wheat.
It is to prevent the spread of noxious weeds t

Yes, that is the difficulty which Is in the way, and I call the hon. gentleman's attention to it. We certainly have no objection to the provision which he suggests but this is the difficulty in the way of its adoption.
What is the advantage of having the dockage in the hands of the merchant more than in the hands of the farmer ? Is it not just as liable to be spread in the country in the one case as in the other ?
It is usually burned.
If you have a provision requiring it to be burned that is all right.

I do not know what the provisions of the Noxious Weeds Act of the North-west Territories are, but my recollection of the Manitoba Act is that it is made an offence to allow the tailings to be taken away from the elevator and they are required to be burned.

So far as that is concerned the elevators of Manitoba have been selling them right along, and I know of cases last winter where they shipped them out of the country. They have been shipping them to Minneapolis.
As long as they ship them to Minneapolis it is all right.

It is a fact that the elevator men are making an undue profit out of these screenings and I do not think the Act of the territorial legislation should stand in the way of this amendment. If the territorial assembly feels disposed to pass an Act that will prohibit this being done, well and good ; but I do not think it applies to the province of Manitoba under the present statute.

I would ask the hon. minister a question in reference to the form of storage receipt in schedule as to the charges for receiving, cleaning, insurance against loss by fire, handling, storing, and so on. I see it says :
It is provided by law that this charge shall
not exceed	dollars of a cent
per bushel.
Is there a stipulated amount for charges mentioned in the Act ?
The amount which the elevator man can charge by this Act is under the regulation of the Governor in Council.
Is it a stipulated amount ?
It is under the control of the Governor In Council.

I know that the farmers consider that this is an excessive charge, although I am not aware what it is. The resolution passed by this investigating committee suggested that the Act should he amended so as to read that the charges shall not exceed one and three-quarter cents per bushel and that they shall be only one and a quarter cents per bushel where the cleaning is not done.
That would be a proper matter to have to consider. I could not very well put in any fixed rate without inquiring, but I can have the attention of the grain commissioner called to the matter.

House again in committee on Bill (No. 98) to incorporate the Montreal Subway Company.-Mr. McCarthy. t
On section 20, subsection (b),

I have an amendment to suggest. I am sorry the promoter of the Bill is not here, but I wish to say that I have had a consultation with some of the promoters of the Bill and they have Horn Mr. SIFTON.
agreed to this amendment with a view of stopping any further opposition, so that the Bill may be able to go through both Houses this session. The amendment reads:
The company shall, within seven months of the passing of this Act, expend on construction work of said subway the sum of $200,000; otherwise the charter will be considered null and void.
The men at the back of this Bill are some of the best men we have in Canada; the Hon. Senator Maekay and others who could build the subway themselves without any outside assistance, but if any accident should happen, so that during the next seven months they do not desire to go on, then it would give some other company an opportunity of advertising a Bill for the next session of parliament, either for a bridge or a tunnel. I am speaking now entirely in the interest of the city of Montreal. We have got to get a bridge or a tunnel at once. I am glad to see some of the members from Montreal here, and I am sure they will back me up in what I say in this regard. We have been waiting for communication between Montreal and the South Shore year after year, and if these people are willing to build this tunnel as they say, without asking the country to assist them in any way, why, of course, we should let them do so, and we should let the bridge people do the same thing under similar conditions. If they are going to build bridges and tunnels to connect Montreal with the South Shore, and not ask the country for subsidies; by all means let them build them, and if possible immediately.
It is not intended as a pleasure road.

It is not a pleasure road no doubt, but I can tell my hon. friend that the farmers on the South Shore are most prosperous; they come every day to the city, and there is a strong feeling in favour of some new communication between the South Shore and the city. That feeling has arisen because they believe the Grand Trunk Railway has not used them liberally enough. They believe that the rates on the Grand Trunk Railway bridge are too high, and so they insist on having a new means of communication. Before this Bill goes through the House, I shall, therefore, insist that the two tunnels will go on together, and I am sure I will be supported in that by all the members from the district of Montreal. Speaking of the amendment just proposed by my hon. friend (Mr. Bickerdike), I may say that I am very glad that he has taken the trouble to consult the promoters of the Bill in Montreal, and I fully agree with him.

This question was fully discussed in the Railway Committee, which came to the conclusion that it would exact from these parties a deposit of $50,000 for their good faith when they would submit their plans to the Governor in Council, and also that $100,000 would be spent by them within nine months. I believe that guarantee is amply sufficient unless you want to kill the project. For my part, I am rather inclined in favour of a bridge, and I have been in favour of a bridge for 20 or 25 years. I know that the citizens of Montreal are in favour of a bridge, but in what position are we at the present time? We are iu the position that we are not likely to have any bridge Bill passed during the present session of parliament. The 142$
only bridge Bill that was submitted to the committee seriously was withdrawn, but there remains another Bill which is on the Order paper for the second reading. If the hon. gentleman who occupies the important position of Minister of Public Works in the government of Canada; if he will undertake to support the other Bill which is the second Order of the day, and if he will undertake to give to the citizens of Montreal and to the people on the South Shore some help as regards improved means of communication with the city, I do not know what I would do myself under the existing conditions. But I do not think that it is possible to have the other Bill passed during this session. If prorogation is going to take place next Tuesday or Wednesday, this other Bill cannot go before the committee until Monday, and there is no knowing when it would come back to the House. Although, as I have said, I am not quite favourable to the tunnel sdheme, yet as a representative of Montreal for the past twenty-five years, and knowing the sentiments of the people there, I know that they want that the promoters of any scheme which will give them communication between the two sides of the river, shall have a chance to go on with the execution of the work which they contemplate.
Not a word has been said against the promoters of this enterprise. There are two or three of them who are certainly in a position to build and to carry to a success this enterprise with their own resources. If they are not serious, or if they discover within the next three months, after having put engineers to work to ascertain what is to be done, that it is impossible, with the amount of capital at their disposal, to carry on the work, there will be nothing lost, and there will be opportunity for any serious company to give the necessary notices and come before parliament next session and ask for the necessary legislation to give them the right to build either a tunnel or a bridge. I repeat that all we want is communication between the two shores of the St. Lawrence; and as a citizen of the city of Montreal, interested in the welfare of the city, and knowing the sentiments of the people, I think we should give every possible chance to this company to become incorporated and to start the necessary works. If you impose upon the company conditions which are impossible, you might as well kill the Bill at once, ana tell the people of Montreal to wait until it pleases us to have this communication between the two shores provided. I say this without any hesitation, knowing, as I have said, exactly the sentiments of the citizens of Montreal. Tne amount required to be deposited, $50,000, as a guarantee of good faith, is a better provision than the one suggested by the hon. member for the St. Lawrence division; because If these people are not serious, they will not risk having the $50,000 forfeited,

whereas people who are not serious might say, ' We will go on and get the plans prepared and submit these plans to the government, and after we have done that, we will spend part of the $200,000, and then try to get an extension of time from parliament.' Then they would come here and say to parliament: 'We have had plans prepared at a cost of, say $50,000, and we have spent $30,000 in making soundings and experiments, and we want an extension of time.' Parliament, being always well disposed, would grant the extension of time for another year; and the result would be that the citizens of Montreal and the people on the south shore of the St. Lawrence would be deprived of the incorporation of a serious company, which would have been in a position to go on with the undertaking. I speak feelingly on this matter, not only as a representative of the city of Montreal, but as one interested in the welfare of the people on the south shore: for I may say that the door of political life was opened, to me by the people of my native county of Chambl'y, and 1 have a great deal of sympathy for them. I know what the farmers of the south shore have been suffering for years; I know the sentiment they have towards an enterprise of this kind. When it was decided by this parliament that half a million should be granted to the Grand Trunk Railway Company to enable it to enlarge the Victoria bridge and to make it a general traffic bridge, as was stated at the time, the project was bailed with rejoicing on both sides of the St. Lawrence; but when it was discovered that instead of it being a traffic bridge, it only gave one-fourth tlie advantages which were expected, the people of the south shore were only pacified by the friends of the government telling them that whenever a serious com-pa ny would undertake to build a bridge or to carry out some other scheme to provide communication between the two shores, it would be given the power to do so. If you now refuse this opportunity to this company, and impose upon it conditions which are impossible, and which will prevent people even thinking of undertaking such a work, you will do an injustice to fifteen or twenty counties on the south shore of the St. Lawrence, as well as to the city of Montreal. I have no hesitation in saying that if the hon. member for the St. Lawrence division were not actuated by good motives, and really thought that 'his' amendment would block the enterprise, I do not think he would persist in it; because the clause ns it stands in the Rill before Ihe House affords all the necessary safeguards to the public ; and next session, if these people prove not to be serious in what they undertake, the field will be perfectly open to another company to come before this House and get another charter.
Surely my hon. friend can have no objection to accept the amendment which has been accepted in Montreal by the most influential promoters of the Bill.
I did not know that before.
My hon. friend from the St. Lawrence division met to-day the hon. Senator Mackay and Mr. Ross
Mr. Miles.

I beg pardon-Senator Mackay and Mr. Miles, and both of them have authorized him to move this amendment. Here is the amendment:
The company shall within seven months of the passing of this Act expend on construction works of said subway the sura of $200,000, otherwise the charter shall he considered null and void.
Does that strike out the necessity of the deposit of $50,000 '!

No. The deposit remains as it is ; but instead of $100,000, which is specified in section 21 of the Bill, the amendment provides that $200,000 shall be spent on construction work. Surely the people of Montreal cannot have any objection to taking every security that it is possible to give. I know that my hon. friend (Mr. Prefontaine) is deeply interested in the welfare of the city of Montreal and the ridings on the south shore; but it has not been by granting charters imprudently that we have served those large interests in the past. We have had on the statute-book for the last ten or twelve years a charter to build a bridge, but it is not built yet. The promoters of fhe undertaking, being substantial men, have approved of the amendment, and under the circumstances, I think it should be accepted.
Is the sum of $200,000 substituted for the sum of $100,000. which was inserted in the Bill by fhe Railway Committee ?
Yes.

The Minister of Public Works is entirely mistaken. According to the amendment, the sum of $200,000 is to be spent within seven months after the passage of the Bill, whereas, if I remember rightly, the Railway Committee decided that the sum of $100,000 should be spent within nine months after the approval of the plans and specifications by the Governor in Council. The two provisions are entirely different.
I am sorry to see the opposition of the hon. Minister of Public Works, for I think

it is the duty of the government to sustain the action of the Railway Committee. As the hon. minister says, most respectable men are the incorporators in this Bill. After full discussion, the committee decided that, as an evidence of their bona tides, $50,000 should toe deposited by the parties who were applying-that is by the incorporators- which, in the event of their not going on with the undertaking, will be forfeited to the Crown, and further, that, on the expiry of nine months after the acceptance or approval of the plans by the Governor in Council, $1,000,000 shall have been expended on the undertaking.
Mr. McCarthy. Make it $200,000 if you like.

Make it $200,000 and then I suppose there will be no objection to the Bill. I draw the attention of the hon. member from St. Lawrence (Mr. Bick-erdike) to the fact that this amendment is completely irregular. He has not given notice of it, and canont move it except with the unanimous consent of the House.
I know that.

I came here to-night to try and get the Bill through, because if we do not get it through to-night it will not go through at all. This is a compromise, which was arrived at yesterday in Montreal, and I ask hon. members to accept it now.
We will do it unanimously, if the hon. member will agree to substitute $200,000 for the $100,000.
I am quite willing.
And provide that it be expended on construction work.

If after the passing of the Bill, when the borings are made, it is found that the company cannot go on, 1 want to give other parties an opportunity to advertise in time to have a Bill introduced next session.
You can advertise whether you are going on or not.
No reasonable men would come in unless they be given the time I ask.

Will not the hon. member for St. Lawrence accept the amendment proposed by the promoters of the Bill to have $200,000 substituted for $100,000 V The hon. gentleman must understand that the promoters cannot commence the work until the plans are approved by the government, and they are only given nine months after the approval of the plans for the expenditure of $200,000. There is a forfeiture of $50,000, to which they are subject, and they have besides to expend $200,000 within nine months after the approval of the plans, under penalty of forfeiture of their charter.
If the hon. gentleman will accept seven months instead of nine months
There are a lot of Bills behind this, and let us get through with it.
I want this to go through.
What the hon. member asks is fairly reasonable.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the committee to substitute $200,000 for the $100,000 provided in the Bill ?

It seems to me that this is too important a Bill to railroad through the committee at the rapid rate at which it is attempted to put it through. We had considerable discussion in the committee over this Bill and a great deal of impatience was shown and a very strong disposition to force it through, whether, in the judgment of many, it was right or wrong. It is a very important undertaking, far reaching in its consequences, and it seems to me that a little delay would be more in, keeping with the best interests of the city of Montreal and the people of that part of the country than to hurry the measure through too rapidly. When this Bill was before the Railway Committee, one of the strongest reasons given in its behalf was the respectability and financial strength of the men whose names appear as its incorporators. But members of parliament, who have been in this House any length of time, have learned to estimate at its proper value this parading of prominent names. We have learned over and over again that these names are simply used for the specific purpose of influencing the House and the committee to get a scheme through, and find out afterwards that the owners of these names had indeed very little to do with it, and very often the charter passes shortly afterwards into the hands of men who are little better than men of straw. Older members do not lay as much stress, as do some of the younger ones, on the importance of these prominent financial names, which are too often lent for the purpose of carrying the Bill through the House. I am not underestimating the financial ability of these men as financiers of Montreal or the Dominion. There is no doubt they command a very large amount of capital. And if their financial wealth were at stake, that would give us a guarantee that they intended to carry the enterprise (through and do not intend to let it pass into other hands. But it is because we know from experience that such is mat always the case and that too often these prominent names are used for the purpose of getting a Bill through the House, and for

that purpose alone, that we do not attach to them the value we otherwise would. It is proposed to make a tunnel under the St. Lawrence, and that suggests the questions whether the scheme is feasible, how much it will cost, when it can be completed, and of what utility it will be when completed. These are the questions we naturally consider in seeking to determine whether it will be wise or otherwise to assist them in putting through this scheme. If we consider what other tunnels have cost and compare them with the proposal in this Bill, we can come to but one conclusion-that the gentlemen who have lent their names to this scheme have taken but little trouble to collect the data which they ought to have for their own guidance and for the use of parliament and of the committee in the discussion of a scheme of this kind. I have a few facts with regard to the cost of the St. Clair tunnel, and this proposed St. Lawrence tunnel, I believe, will be a great deal more expensive. The St. Clair tunnel cost $3,324,000

I rise to a point of order. Are we going to have a dissertation on the cost of every tunnel in America as part of the discussion of this Bill, when there are twenty Bills on the Order paper awaiting the attention of the committee ?
That makes no difference.
It surely is not germane to the question to discuss the cost of tunnels elsewhere.

On the question of order, I venture to submit that the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Sproule's) remarks are quite pertinent to the question. It is most important to consider whether this tunnel really will be built, and the information the hon. gentleman is giving is relevant to the question and important in consideration of it. I do not think the point of order is well taken.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) is quite within ihis rights.

I was sure you would make such a ruling, Mr. Speaker, for it would be unprecedented to deny the right to present legitimate arguments such as I am presenting in connection with this matter. It must not be forgotten that this can only pass this House by unanimous consent. Any member- has a right to object to the amendment if he desires to do so. The fact that we do not act upon that right shows the indulgence we are inclined to exercise towards the hon. gentleman's scheme.
Will the hon. gentleman allow me to ask him a question ?
Yes.

If the promoters accept the condition of the expenditure of $200,000 within nine months and the deposit of $50,000, does not the hon. gentleman think that a sufficient guarantee that these people are in earnest ?
I would consider it better than the $50,000 alone. But It is not enough to satisfy me that they
How much do you want ?

I am opposed to the principle of a tunnel, for the reasons that I propose to give to the House. In the first place, I say the cost is very much greater than the promoters of this Bill have estimated it to be. and that would be one of the strongest deterrents to the fruition of the scheme. I was about to say that the St. Olair tunnel, which is a single tunnel with a single track and which is only twenty feet in diameter, which is through clay thirty feet below the water at the lowest point, the approach grade being only two per cent on one side-while this St. Lawrence tunnel is two per cent one side and steeper on the other-cost $3,234,857. Now, if this St. Lawrence tunnel is to give the accommodation to the public the promoters profess a desire to give, it would require not one tunnel but two or three-
Two tunnels.
This would make the cost at least twice as great as the ,St. Clair tunnel, that is to say, the cost would run up to about $7,000,000, even if it were no greater in length than the St. Clair tunnel.
What is the length of the St. Clair tunnel ?

The open cut on the Canadian side is 3,270 feet; tunnel on the Canadian side, 1,160 feet; tunnel under the river, 2,310 feet; on the American side, 1,810 feet ; open cut on the American side, 2,820 feet-total, 11,370 feet, or 2-23-100 miles. The proposed St. Lawrence tunnel is 4-11-100 miles in length. Thus, besides requiring two tubes, this tunnel is nearly twice as long as the St. Clair tunnel. I think we have every reason to believe that it will be proportionately as costly, and, on that basis, the expense involved will be about $15,000,000. We must take this item of cost into consideration, in deciding whether it is wise or not to give the promoters the right to build this tunnel. For, the existence of this charter, even if the work were not carried out, would have the effect of preventing the building [DOT] of a bridge which, to my mind, would be much better. Now I have the figures here concerning the Washington tunnel in Chicago. That is a dry tunnel. It was built in 1867 for general traffic. But it was very unpopular and was never used to any great extent. We are

told by the promoters of this Bill that this St. Lawrence tunnel would be as useful for traffic as a bridge. Any one who knows anything about tunnels knows that that is perfect moonshine. What benefit would it be to the farmers of the south shore if they have the tunnel built 7 Practically none at all, for they could not use it for general traffic to any great extent. The Washington tunnel was turned over to the' street railway in 1890. It consists of two arches with centre walls, approach grade seven to eight per cent, with a length of open cut of 570 feet and tunnel 930 feet, a total of 1,500 feet. It was very costly, but I need not go into the figures, as that part of it does not bear any relation to this. Now, what is proposed for this St. Lawrence tunnel 7 They propose to build a tunnel open at the north side for 2,500 feet, against 3,370 feet for the St. Clair tunnel. There will be a land tunnel of 6,800 feet. The river tunnel will be 5,500 feet, whereas the river tunnel under the St. Clair is only 2,310 feet. I give these figures to show how much more expensive this one will be and how much more imporant this enterprise will be, than even the St. Clair tunnel which took such a long time to put through. The land on the south side would be 2,630 feet, the open cut would be 4.220 feet; in all the total cut with the tunnel would be 21,700 feet, while the St. Clair tunnel had only 11.370 feet. Now, when these figures are remembered one can understand what it means to build a tunnel under the St. Lawrence down at Montreal. But they are going to double track this tunnel, it is going to be 26 feet wide and 23 feet high. The estimated cost, without the land damages, will be $3,500,000. The cost of the St. Clair tunnel for a single tube was over $3,234,000. You see the enormous disparity between the sizes of the tunnels, and yet the one is to cost about the same as the other. It shows how little time has been spent in making up the estimate, on what slight data a conclusion has been based of the cost of this tunnel. This tunnel would cost at least $13,500,000, and it is to require three years to build it. If we may judge from the rapidity with which these tunnels have been built in the past it is more likely to take four or five years to build it than three years.
Now, it will not give the same accommodation as a bridge would give, and in my judgment a bridge is the only feasible scheme there in the interests of the people, because we want the common people to be able to use it as well as the railway companies. The railway companies can use a tunnel all right but the ordinary foot passenger cannot use it, and the man with a horse and vehicle cannot use it. I asked the question in the Railway Committee, how is the man going there with his produce to get through the tunnel ? It has to be put on a car, horse and all, and carried
through. When you consider the amount of traffic from one side of the river to the other you can understand how many will use it. It will require three tunnels similar to this one to give the same convenience to the people as a bridge would give, and three tunnels at the estimated cost given by the hon. gentleman for this one would cost $10,500,000. And what I have given you with reference to the actual facts of building the St. Clair tunnel justifies the conclusion that instead of its costing $15,000,000 it would cost nearer $20,000,000 or $30,000,000, and I have no doubt it will when it comes to be built.
Now, the time they require to build it in is three years, as against two years for a bridge. We are told, and I think we are justified in believing that a bridge could easily be built inside of two years. But it would be utterly impossible to push on a tunnel at the ordinary progress usually made in building tunnels in anything like that time. For these reasons I am opposed to a tunnel entirely. But if we must have a tunnel, then I want to say, in view of these prominent names that are paraded with their financial strength as a justification for us to give them this charter, that we want the very strongest binding clauses that can possibly be put in to satisfy us that these men are prepared to put their own money into it, to go on at once and build this tunnel and not keep it for speculative purposes and sell out to the first man that comes along. * I am opposed to it in the next place because, considering the gigantic nature of the undertaking, I do not think it is likely to be carried through. I am opposed to it because I do not think we have sufficient data to enable us to determine whether it would be wise for us to pass this Bill. Has there been a boring made in the St. Lawrence river to show what the sub soil is like ? Has there been any engineering investigation; anything more than an ordinary estimate ? Nothing, so far as I know, nothing that was before the committee; so we are really going it blind. I am opposed to it, as I said, because it involves an immense expenditure of money which is not likely to be made inside the next four or five years.
But thes.e gentlemen do not ask us for any money. I want that fact to be kept in mind. The promoters of the Bill told us the other day that they do not ask us for a subsidy.

I am not taking that into account at all. I am discussing the feasibility of the scheme, the probability of its being carried out, and the importance of it after it is built; and I am drawing a comparison between the value of that scheme to the people both on the north shore and the south shore, and the value of a bridge, and I reach the conclusion in my own mind

that if this tunnel is undertaken it will destroy the probability of a bridge ever being built for a long time to come. These are the points of view from which I am discussing the scheme at the present time. Now, the expenditure on the tunnel is to be very large, and these names are put forward as a reason why it is going to be built. I do not wish to underestimate the value and the financial importance of these names, because I believe they are all respectable men, all men of wealth and men who can control a great deal of money with their influence, if they desire to do so. Therefore if they are bona fide and going to invest their own capital and are not asking parliament to give them any subsidy why, they should have, it is said, an opportunity to build it. But it is because I believe they do not intend to build it that I am speaking against this Bill.
How do you know ?

I am giving reasons why I come to that conclusion. I do not say I know, but I say I am justified in coming to that conclusion for the reasons that I have given. Then again I say, in conclusion, that the tunnel is of no use for ordinary traffic purposes. What are the chief requirements for the ordinary farmer on the south shore ? It is to get over the river cheaply and readily to reach that great and valuable market. Are they going to get there through the tunnel 1 Farmers do not use the St. Clair tunnel, they do not use any other tunnel for that purpose that I know of. Why ? Because they cannot use it with safety, they cannot use it with convenience, they cannot use it without very great danger, and they are not likely to use it at all. We are told that these tunnels, filled as they are with trains passing back and forth, with smoke, gas and foul air, not lighted, not properly ventilated, that they cannot be used by the ordinary travelling public at all. What benefit will it be to the farmer ? I am talking on behalf of the poor farmer that wishes to get to this market. I spoke on exactly the same lines when the Victoria bridge was being widened and I did my level best then to get a clause put in that Bill that would protect the travelling public against exorbitant charges I was fought on that line by members who advocated the scheme. And what was the result after the bridge was built ? Why we had the representatives of the people coming back and saying that the charges were most exorbitant. It is in view of that experience that I desire to take time by the forelock and not allow the poor habitants to be bound up for all time to come without being able to take advantage of the convenience which they desire for the purpose of getting to that important market. I say If that tunnel is built it will be of no value to the farmer on the south shore, but if a bridge is built it will be of immense value.

I wish the government to keep in their hands the right to reduce the tolls, and to say they shall not be so onerous that the ordinary habitant cannot take advantage of the tunnel. For these reasons I am opposed to the tunnel in toto. But if this House must pass this Bill, then I want to see it passed with the most stringent provisions that will guarantee the building of it at an early day, because as long as this Bill remains it will prevent the possibility of any corporation taking up the scheme of building a bridge across that river, which would be by all means the most valuable communication for the poor people who require it the most.

Before this Bill is carried I would like to make a few remarks as representing one of the south shore counties, the county of Nicolet.
I live in the town of Nicolet. The Quebec Southern road is going to pass through Longueuil and then try to get across, and as one interested, I would like if something else should be built there besides a tunuei. I am getting a little old and I would like to cross over either by a tunnel or a bridge before I die. Why is it that there is a discussion to-day about a tunnel ? There was no talk of a tunnel a few months ago. There was only talk of building the Montreal bridge. Everything was prepared for the building of a bridge ; soundings were made, plans drawn and capitalists were ready to undertake the work. I am told that the owner of the charter had an offer for the sale of that charter. There were capitalists from the United States who desired to purchase it but they could not succeed in the negotiation. I will tell hon. gentlemen why. I was surprised the other night to hear my hon. friend from Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux) say that he was in favour of a bridge, but after making a close investigation he found that a man by the name of Armstrong, was interested in the scheme. Well, it was not the case. He was playing upon the word. There was an Armstrong interested but it was not Mr. O. N. Armstrong, as he wanted to make hon. gentlemen think it was. Mr. Prefontaine

The hon. member for Terrebonne and the hon. member for Maison-neuve (Mr. PrCfontaine). As he was not acting as a member, I have a right to name him. I name him as a partner in this project. Have I a right, Mr. Chairman, to name a man when he is a partner and when I am speaking about his affairs and not speaking about him as a member of this House ?

Some hon. A1EMBERS. Order, order.

The hon. member for Mai-sonneuve bought the notes. They went at a cent on the dollar, and the hon. member for Terrebonne sued Mr. C. N. Armstrong and got judgment against him. Later on he sued his son to nullify the transfer and to retain the shares in the hands of Air. C. N. Armstrong. The court dismissed his case; he could not seize the shares, so he relinquished the whole thing and made an arrangement with other parties-I do not know if I can name that word-schemer- who made application for a tunnel and for a bridge so as to kill that charter that had only to be revived and in regard to which all the preliminary work was done. They tried and with success to kill the charter that only required reviving.
