House again in committee on Bill (No. 119), further to amend the Yukon Territory Act.- The Minister of the Interior.

The hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) furnished me with a draft of some amendments to the clause which I read when we were in the committee on the Bill before. I see no objection to the draft which was given me by my hon. friend except one. Inadvertently the words ' commissioner in council ' are inserted.
speakername: The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR (Hon. Clifford Sifton).

speechtext:
Yes.
The A1INISTER OF THE INTERIOR. Subsection (e) reads as follows :
Provide! always, however, that no ordinance made under this Act imposing a tax or royalty o- any matter relating thereto shall be, or be deemed to he retroactive, &e.
My hon. friend will see that that clause is not practicable, because it will apply to all the grants which are already made, and so will be retroactive. At present we have, under the Dominion Lands Act, imposed a royalty of 5 per cent, and we intend to abolish that royalty and impose a general tax of 2} per cent. We are asking for this legislation because we intend to collect in another way, and we do not think we have power to make provision for the collection without legislative authority. If we abolish the present royalty and undertake to fix a royalty under this Act, subject to the provision that it shall not be retroactive, I am afraid they will be able to say that they have escaped from the royalty which had been levied on them before, and that under this Act we could not impose a royalty upon them. We cannot retroactively apply anything which would be any higher than 5 per cent, and that, no doubt, will meet the object which my hon. friend has in view. It would not affect the rights of any person who has acquired rights under contract from the government.
I would not think the word ' retroactive ' would have the meaning the hon. gentleman suggests.
It might not, but it would be very unfortunate if it were so held.
There have been some questions pending.

The last section is quite sufficient to protect any questions pending, which are all in the shape of suits in the court. It is in respect to past transactions that the questions have arisen, and the royalty of 2i per cent would be a new transaction. There is absolutely nothing in the questions between the government and any person in respect to the royalty, except a few suits that were brought on the ground that we had collected royalty in 1897 when we were not supposed to do so; that our officers commenced too soon to collect royalty. That is the only question pending, and that is before the Exchequer Court.
Is it not a very usual principle that no provision of this kind should be made retroactive ?

But if we abolish the 5 per cent tax and put another tax in place of it, we might be I in the position that there was a limitation in this clause, and it might be held that we could only apply the tax subsequently.

That might not be the case, hut I do not think that the government should take any chances.

I would not wish to leave the legislation in any uncertainty that might make the future collection of taxes doubtful. I am as anxious to avoid that as the hon. gentleman. But is not that matter made perfectly plain under the provisions of the Interpretation Act, which I presume would apply to ordinances made under the provisions of a statute. The hon. gentleman is aware that under the provisions of the Interpretation Act, when we repeal a statute the new provisions shall take effect, and every matter and thing shall be carried on just as if the amending Act had originally been in force instead of the repealed Act. Would not that prevent any such difficulty as the minister suggests?
The'MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR. I do not think so.
Why could it not be made perfectly plain by adding a proviso to the effect that this shall not in any way affect the substitution of the new tax for the old tax?

All we get power to do is to levy a royalty. That is going to affect all, whether the leases are issued at the present time or any past leases or subsequent leases. We intend as soon as this legislation becomes law to pass an ordinance levying a royalty on the gold output of the Yukon Territory, and we intend immediately before doing so to repeal the present Orders in Council, under which the royalty of 5 per cent is collected. We want the legislation to put us in such a position that there can be absolutely no question about it. There is no mine at present in the Yukon which claims in any way to be exempt from royalty except under the exemptions which the royalty Orders in Council provide at the present time. What we have decided to do is that instead of the exemption and a royalty of 5 per cent, there shall be a general tax of 2J per cent. We do not want any doubt to exist as to our right to do that. I can assure my hon. friend that there is no question at the present time except with respect to certain claims which arise out of the Act of 1897. We desire to have the legislation in such a position that there cannot be any possible ground for litigation after the Order in Council has passed.
The new tax will take effect from the date of the new Order in Council ?
Yes.
Is not the government perfectly protected by providing in the new Order in Council that the old tax shall continue in force until a particular

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: day. after which the new tax shall take effect ?

I do not think so. The very fact that there is doubt about it is the reason we are asking for legislation. We unquestionably have power to impose a royalty under the 'Dominion Lands Act; but I doubt if we have power to impose it in the form in which we desire to do it. that is. as a royalty to be collected at the boundary line instead of at the mine. We have to take certain proceedings in order to collect, the royalty in that way, which we have not the power to do by Order in Council without special legislation, and that is the reason why we are asking for this legislative power. If we could justify it under the old law. this Act would not be necessary. There is a question of some hundreds of thousands of dollars of revenue involved, and if we lost even half a million dollars, we could not go back on our legislation if we made a mistake or took any chances. The rest of the clause, as my hon. friend has drawn it, I am quite agreeable to accept; and I think I can suggest what would perhaps meet my liou. friend's wishes and not incur any danger, that is. to add to subsection ' a ' a clause like this :	Imposing a tax or
royalty not exceeding 5 per cent thereof on gold and silver the output of the mines of the territory, to be levied from and after the date of the ordinance. That could not be the subject of any doubt. It could not be retroactive.
I think that would assist.

I would like to point out to the hon. minister that the last subsection of the amendment only applies to suits now pending. If it is to have the effect he thinks it ought to have, it should have words added which would include any cause of action which has not yet begun.
We will make it read : ' Any cause of action now accrued or any matter or suit now pending in any court.'

There is one other matter I would like to mention. Under section 2 of this Bill, the commissioner in council has the same powers of legislation with respect to the Yukon territory, which the government of the North-west Territories have with respect to the North-west Territories. Then under another clause the Governor in Council has the power to make certain ordinances respecting the Yukon Territory, and I would like to know whether or not these powers conflict in any way.

A clause has been drawn by the Department of Justice providing that in case of conflict the ordinances of the Governor in

Council will prevail. As matters are at present, there will be very little necessity for the Governor in Council taking action. That would only happen in some special emergency, and in case of conflict, in order to avoid unnecessary litigation, we provide that the ordinances of the Governor in Council shall prevail. Of course we have the power of vetoing any ordinances, and the effect of the clause will be simply to avoid any unnecessary litigation.

That is to say there is a power of veto which can be ex-, ercised. I have one more suggestion ; would the hon. gentleman have any objection to qualifying clause 6 by adding some such provision as we have added to clause 3 1

We are not giving them anything which they have not at present practically. The only thing we could add would be a clause similar to what they use in the American States, providing that there shall be no interference with vested rights, but we are simply following the legislation in connection with the North-west Territories, and no difficulty has arisen there. They simply deal with questions of property and civil rights of a local kind.

I am inclined to think that there is a clause which covers that objection.
Bill, as amended, reported; read the third time, and passed.

House in Committee of Supply.
Charges of management-Additional sum required for clerical assistance in connection with the issue and redemption of Dominion notes, $1,000.
['Yes.\nSome resolutions reported.']

We had to take a supplementary vote for the current year, making our appropriation for this year $7,300. We are asking now an appropriation which will make the vote for next year $8,000. This is owing to the fact that the increase of circulation makes necessary additions to the clerical staff.
You are saving that much interest.
I thought these Dominion notes were issued by the American Bank Note Company.

My hon. friend is confusing this with the item of printing. The notes are printed and supplied to us by the American Bank Note Company, the contractors. But, however great may be our confidence in that company, we would hardly entrust them with the signing and issuing of these notes. This money is to pay for clerical assistance in countersigning the notes and superintending the issue. This is work largely performed by young 'ladies who receive, I am sorry
to say, not very large salaries-from $400 to $600.

The
point is that this salary has already been provided for. But the object here is to promote this officer.

The
other could be dropped on concurrence. I suppose ; at the same time there is a little difficulty in that. I can give the House the assurance that it is not the intention to pay more than one salary. But I would not like to change the vote in the absence of the minister. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) wishes to have the.item stand, there will be no objection.
I do not think this is a very good way of putting the appropriation. Perhaps it would be better to let it stand.

Very well, let it stand until the Minister of Railways arrives.

Civil government-Department of Trade and Commerce-To provide for one senior second-class clerk, $1,100.

This is made necessary by the fact that the Department of Trade and Commerce is taking over work from the Department of Inland Revenue, such as the inspection of staples and the grain inspection.

But,

an increase in the Department of Inland Revenue.

Auditor General's oiBee-To provide for the salary of a junior second-class clerk, eontin-gencies, clerical and other assistance; printing and stationery, $3,600.

The Auditor General requires extra assistance, and we are glad to give it to him. He has been rather sharply criticised for not doing enough; I think he is disposed to do a little more and make his book a little larger.

Mr. Desrochers is an old and valuable employee whom I have just promoted.

The details of this work are as follows : Administration building, filling up swamp and making sidewalk, $6,000; post office, filling swamp and grading, $5,000; furniture, $1,000; government house, filling in and fencing sidewalk, $3,000; court house, $2,.000; mining inspectors' offices in four places, $15,000; furniture. They will complete the erection and equipment of public buildings out there.
Will the revenue from the Yukon pay all this money we are spending this year ?

Yes. Without reference to a particular year, the expenditures in the Yukon have been less than our revenue up to the present date. I am not quite sure as to any particular year, but the aggregate expenditure is less than the aggregate of our receipts In the Yukon up to the present. The Minister of the Interior has announced that he is going to make a reduction in the royalty. We are hopeful that even with the reduced rate, we shall continue to receive enough to pay all the expenses. The very fact that we have received already a larger sum than we have expended Is fair ground why we should reduce the royalty; because, while we are anxious to make the Yukon pay for the Yukon, we are not desirous of making a profit out of it. We are hopeful that under the new system for the collection of the royalty at the reduced rate, it will still yield us a liberal revenue, enough to meet all the expenses.
I telegraphed Mr. Bertrand and he replied saying that Louise Collinet and her husband had been dismissed because they had declined to obey orders. That is nil I know about the case.

I do not know what explanation the resident architect offers of his letter in winch he says :
You will continue therefore, to he at the service of Mr. Justice Dugas, and act under his guidance for any work which you shall be required to Jo as matron of the court house.

What had these people to do with Judge Dugas in regard to their meals ?

They were transferred from the Department of the Interior to the Department of Public Works, and up to that date they had been paid only, respectively, $80 and $60 per month. Later on, they were 'given additional salary, but they were supplied with lodgings and rations. Later on again they did not get lodgings or rations. Then they were placed on the same footing as oilier charwomen and caretakers, the wife receiving $150 a month and being free to arrange for her meals anywhere she liked. I apprehend that she made an arrangement with Mr. Justice Dugas to board at his place, and it looks very much as if she had paid her board to Mr. Justice Dugas. I am not here to defend the judge. It is not my business. I state the facts as I understand them. It is not my business to defend that arrangement. I have nothing to do with that. All I want to state is that my department followed towards these people the ordinary course. As to the arrangement with Judge Dugas, it is for him to say whether it is proper or not. I have nothing to do with that.
I do not see an explanation of the order given by the chief architect to tills matron that she should be at the service of Mr. Justice Dugas. He does not explain that.

Yes, he explains that in his report. The mounted police had arranged that the caretaker and charwoman would take care of Mr. Justice Dugas' lodging rooms. He was in the mounted police apartments then. AVlien he went to other quarters, the same arrangement continued. Rightly or wrongly, it continued. But, it won't happen again, lfecause. thank God, I am getting rid of the whole thing. The commissioner of the Yukon will settle that himself. In looking over the expenditure in connection with Yukon public buildings for the past year, I observe that some of the practices which have prevailed in regard to Mr. Justice Dugas have not by any means been confined to him. I am responsible, of course ; but I want to state again that this was not my own personal policy ; but the government decided for a time to erect residences for the judges. We found it was too expensive, and in the meantime we paid for their rentals and the maintenance of their houses. Whether it was right or wrong, of course 1 am fully responsible, but let it be understood that it is not my personal responsibility alone.

I am not criticising the hon. gentleman ; I am criticising the government, and I am under-stating the matter. Suppose the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Finance, in addition to the salaries they enjoy as servants of this government, were allowed $3,000 or $5,000 for living expenses, and in addition took money voted for public buildings iu Ontario and with it provided themselves with residences here in Ottawa, furnished those residences, and paid for coal and electric lights for themselves : they would be in exactly the same position as the two judges, the Gold Commissioner and the Commissioner of the Yukon. It seems to me a very inequitable proceeding to give a judge of the Yukon such extraordinary emoluments, which are denied judges In the older provinces, who have no doubt to maintain larger establishments. In Nova Scotia you limit a judge to a salary of about $4,000 or $5,000, and I am bound to say that the man whom you sent out to the Yukon is not equal in

So that this country must look to the establishment of a fast line and at the same time to the establishment of a line of carriers. The sooner we in Canada realize that we must stand on our own bottom the better.

I have noticed in the press of late an intimation that there are some important negotiations going on in England by Lord Strathcona in regard to this fast Atlantic service, and the plan which the hon. ministei; has outlined would indicate that he- imagines there is some possibility of the project being realized at an early date. Has he any information to give the House in regard to what is being done in view of the fact that there appears to be a combine of the carrying trade of the Atlantic at the present time, and can he tell us what steps the government are taking to prevent the possibility of any line that is established being absorbed by the combine ?

I do not see that the government can do much to prevent the shareholders in any existing company selling their shares if they see fit. That is the great trouble. We have nothing to say, we can do nothing.
If you subsidize a line of steamers, can you not attach conditions to that subsidy ?

I am speaking of the past and as to the future the Prime Minister could speak if he were here. I have no doubt we will take good care that our subsidies are not lost.

I have the greatest holies that at the imperial conference this question will be discussed and solved in the interest of the empire and the colonies. I expect the greatest results from that conference.
Mr. SPROU1.E. What will be the length and depth of that wall ?
1.200 feet on one side and 410 feet on the other.
What will it be built of ?

Concrete and cement, and crib-work under structure. I believe we have made a great mistake in using crib-work in the past. Its average life out of water is between seven and eight years and the outside life ten years.
What is the life of it below water ?

Eternity, unless there is some accident or unless worms eat the timber, and in future we will creosote all timber where there are worms. I am taking a vote for a creosoting plant.
accommodate thirty vessels at a time and he would have a port which would last for ever, and which would not cost him so much as this patch work which he now proposes and which is always very expensive. The present basin at Quebec cost $5,000,000 or $6,000,000, and it is practically of no use whatever. Vessels can only go in and out when the tide is high, so that they have to wait seven hours a day. which is a great delay in view of the expedition which our trade requires at the present day. If you build a wall down from the St. Charles river you can accommodate all the vessels you like and you can build all the railway tracks that are necessary. Clear down to the Montrribreney falls, at the mouth of the Beauport river, there is a splendid bottom, and the water is quite deep, and you could build the wall along-there, and you would not have to dredge much. You could establish a port there that you and your children and the whole country could be proud of. You would not be wasting money patching here and there, but you would be spending money to good advantage. The wall we have built has moved about three feet and sunk in the basin. It is a dangerous place.

The Minister of Public Works admits himself that there was a great mistake made in placing this basin at Quebec. I am surprised, however, thaMhe minister has not learned something from the mistakes made in the past. I believe that if he carries out the project he has now in view he will commit a bigger sin than lias been committed by his predecessors in office. The hon. gentleman has the bad example of others right before his eyes, but yet ho has learned nothing from experience and he proposes to follow out that bad example. He is going to build a little crib-work there and he will have two or three small boats in the harbour and to do that he will have to dredge in the river and blast the rocks, and he may spend $1,000,000 or $2,000,000.
There is no rock there at all.

I know there are no floating rocks but there are rocks down below. If the minister intends to make a decent port at Quebec, why does he not go right below the St. Charles river and build a straight wall to the asylum at Beauport ? If the minister does.that he will have one of the best ports in Canada and there will be all the facilities for shipping that can be required. If the minister of Public Works commences at the St, Charles river, he can build his wall or wharf and go clear down to the insane asylum if he wishes.
Hear, hear.

There is an insane asylum about two miles below, and I am perfectly right in saying that he can extend down to the asylum. There is no joke about that matter at all. If the minister would adopt the suggestion that I am making, he could
Mr. BOYD". Refore that item passes. I think it is well that the minister should give us some explanation in regard to it. I supposed, when the hon. gentleman was making his explanations. that at last we had got part of some well defined scheme of transportation to meet the present emergency, especially in the western portion of the country: but after listening to the practical remarks of the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Morin), we find that, instead of any well-defined scheme, we have what he describes as a tumble-down portion of what is impracticable. I am tired of this little patching of wharfs and the indiscriminate expenditure of money all over this country in the manner in which it has been done by this government for some time past: and it is time that the government realized a sense of the duty they owe to the country, and arranged some well-defined and well-matured plan to meet the emergency of that western country that is staring us in the face.

I have great confidence in the judgment of my hon. friend from Dorchester. He is a practical man, whose experience seems to have convinced my hon. friend from the west that we do not know much about carrying out these works. But let me say to my hon. friend that the carrying out of his plan might come later on, when trade developes more, and when the building of these long piers might become a necessity. But they would cost a vast amount of money.
Not much.

Let my hon. friend have some confidence in those who have given great attention to

euch matters. It is not tlie first time I have heard of that project. I was in Quebec for 18 years, and I know about that wharf. Beyond a doubt it would cost a large amount of money; and I think in the meantime the country will be contented [DOT]with the moderate expenditure we are making to provide accommodation for four or five steamers. At the same time, my hon. friend from the west should not speak in that wild way, if I may be allowed to say so, accusing us of giving no attention to the west.
I did not say that.

I am glad to hear that he did not. I think we are providing to-day a pretty general plan of transportation. Let my hon. friend look at what is taking place. The two great railway companies, the Canadian Northern and the Canadian Pacific Railway, are adding five or six million bushels capacity to their elevators. There are elevators being built or in sight in nearly every harbour on the Georgian Bay: in Montreal the Harbour Commissioners are building a large elevator; the Grand Trunk Railway is applying for space to build an elevator of 1,000.000 bushels capacity. There are elevators springing up everywhere. We have today passed a Bill which would not have been passed if the House were not kind to the west. It was a pretty hard Bill to swallow.
Will it do any harm to the east ?
No, I think it will do good to the east. But every member of parliament will admit that it is an exceptional Bill. I am strongly in favour of it.
What Bill is it ?

The Grain Bill. It is a very important Bill. We are doing what we can, and we think that by completing our St. Lawrence route, and deepening and equipping our canals, we are going to secure for the west cheap transportation. When we have on the Atlantic ocean the large carriers that I expect to see, and the fast line established, which may be before many years, our equipment will be complete. We are doing now the work that any progressive government would do. We are equipping all our harbours on the St. Lawrence; we are helping the equipment of our harbours on the Georgian Bay; we are deepening the Kaministiquia river; we are deepening Port Arthur; the Canadian Pacific Railway is going to add greatly to its rolling stock and its tracks; the Canadian Northern is also adding to its equipment. We think we are going as fast as we can be expected to go. I know that my views are not shared by everybody ; but I am confident that within two years our Canadian, system of railways and water-Hon. Mr. TARTE.
ways will be in such a position that we shall be able to give cheaper rates to the west than the Americans can. We have the shortest route; we have only to make it the best in order to give cheap rates to our friends in the North-west; and this will help us to establish a Canadian marine, which will employ a large number of men and help to build up our cities, as Buffalo and other American ports have been built up.

I would like to give my advice to the minister, who can. of course, take it or not as he pleases. The minister said he would patch up that basin at Quebec, and then probably go on and build a wall or wharf towards the insane asylum; but he said that at present he did not wish to spend too much money. Well, I will tell him just about what will happen in a year or two if he does not go on with this wharf now. If he occupies the position he does, he will feel afraid to commence it. If somebody else occupies his place he will want to wait a year or two before going on. But the way to do is to make a beginning, and keep on year after year until the work is finished. If you keep patching here and there, all the time afraid to commence the work, you will never build it. The minister also said it would be expensive. That is cofrect; but what will the wharf be worth when it is built ? You will not be sinking money uselessly, but you will be building a wharf and getting value for your expenditure.

I think the hon. Minister of Public Works cannot say that he has received any strenuous or factious opposition from me towards any of the schemes he has propounded in this House. As regards the opinion he may have of myself or other members from the west, or of our breezy manner of putting things, that is immaterial.
I have a very good opinion.

Well, the opinion of the minister is reciprocated by myself. The other evening the hon. minister was haying a discussion in regard to matters of this kind with the hon. member for Saskatchewan. And he waxed rather warm in regard to what this government had done and was doing for the people of the west. Now, I do not know what the Liberal members of the House think of what lias been done by this government for the west in the way of any large expenditure, but I fail to see where any great efforts have been put forth which has caused this country any expense. The Canadian Pacific Railway and all connected with it are no part of the administration of this government. The Canadian Northern got a slight bonus from this government on its Ontario division some two years ago. Apart from that, I do not know of anything that the hon. gentleman can accuse us of having received.

During all that time we from the west have been sitting here voting millions of dollars upon the waterways of this country.
For our common benefit.

Perhaps, but the discussions in this House on many of these public works would not bear out that assumption. We may be accused of being somewhat aggressive and enthusiastic about our country, but it is estimated that at present only one-seventietli of that great country is being cultivated. When we recognize that fact and recognize also that people are pouring in there at present by the thousand, it behooves this government to be on the alert for the future. I was under the impression that at last we were going to receive some of the benefits of the many suggestions thrown out from this side of the House, and that some well considered plan of transportation, to prepare for the great emergency that is awaiting the people of eastern Canada, would have been submitted for our approval. Hon. members speak of the great crop in the west last year, but I have known of three or four better crops in Manitoba. Our average in that province last year was about 22 bushels to the acre. I myself have grown 28, find we have had a better average on two or three previous occasions. There was a better average in the North-west Territories, but we need not look to last year's crop as something exceptional. We are liable to have a greater crop at any time, and with increased cultivation and our enormous acreage, it behooves the government to prepare for a much larger export from that country than we have hitherto had.
Port Colborne-Harbour improvements, $100,000.
What progress is being made at Port Colborne ?

There are about 1,200 feet of breakwater built out of 5,000 feet, but I may say that this amount is not adequate for the completion of the work we have been' authorized to carry out. If hon. gentlemen will follow me, I will explain on this map what is being done. When the plans for the breakwater were prepared, my engineers were of the opinion that it was necessary to have a breakwater 40 feet wide. I was away on the other side of the ocean when the plans were finally adopted. My hon. friend and colleague, the Postmaster General was acting for me. After mature consideration, he made up his mind that 25 feet wide was sufficient. Well, the waves of Lake Erie are just as heavy as those on the Atlantic ocean, and during a gale in the month of February the breakwater moved a couple of inches. I am now asking for $100,000 to add 25 feet width to the breakwater, so as to make the width 50 feet. About 10 or 15
days ago, in another gale, the breakwater was moved about 2 feet, and it is imperative to complete that work. Of course, it will not cost more now than it would have had the original plans prepared by my engineers been adopted. When this breakwater is completed 5,000 feet long, it will give all this area which is marked on the map to tiie large ships that will come to load and unload in the canal. The Minister of Railways and Canals is dredging the entrance of the canal. We shall not be as well equipped as Buffalo, for they have 5 miles of breakwater, and 50 elevators. We have already received application for sites for elevators from private corporations. I do not know what our policy will be, but, in the meantime we are preparing the ground. This year, Mr. Woolvin, who is undertaking to carry grain to Quebec, will use a part of the breakwater. He will have a floating elevator to tranship his grain from large carriers on the lake to small craft that will go to Quebec.
What is the addition to be built of ?
Timber, with a concrete top.
Above the water ?
Yes, about seven feet above the water.
How long does the minister expect it will take to complete the work ?

I must give the contract without an hour's delay, because our breakwater is exposed and I am afraid of another storm. One thing that has helped to save it is that Messrs. I-Iogan & Macdonald, the contractors, have wintered a large quantity of stone inside the breakwater.

The breakwater ought to lie completed next year. It was reasonably light, but the minister says he will strengthen it by putting a concrete wall inside that will make it pretty strong. The whole breakwater should be completed next year ; it must be completed by that time.
It will be, there is no doubt about that.
There are some other matters in connection with the inside harbour that must be discussed later. But, so far as the breakwater is concerned this will be all right.
That means it will be completed in two years ?

No, completed for next season. The contractors have large quantities of ipaterial on hand and a good organization. I was there about the time of the opening of parliament, three months ago and saw xvhat they were doing.
Is the contract let ?
No, I speak of the first contract.
Is that part built of crib-work with a concrete top ?

Unfortunately no. I believe that in that we
made a mistake, and that it should 'have been built in concrete. Of course, it costs a little more money. But. in future, I will ask parliament. in all these large public works, to allow me to use the best materials, because they are the cheapest in the end. As I have said, the outside life of the wooden structure above water is ten years and the ordinary life is between seven and eight years. In Buffalo they made the same mistake that we have made. But now, they are building with large blocks of stone.

The minister, no doubt, is proceeding upon information which he regards as justifying his course. But it does not appear to me that the best plan is to build with cement on top of crib-work. There must be the same liability of the wood decaying.
Wood never will decay under water.
How many hundred years has the hon. gentleman lived to be able to determine that 1

I do not need to live five years to determine that. If the cribs are absolutely under water they are safe from decay for nil time to come. That is the testimony of all engineers, and you can only proceed in these matters on what you are told by the best engineers in tilie country. They will tell you that cribs sunk under water with a concrete fop make the best breakwater or dam that you can put in - the cheapest and the best.
That may lie very valuable. but the hon. member (Sir. German) will hardly expect us to take it upon his experience.
Let the hon. gentleman (Sir. Sproule) ask any engineer.
It is a fact-if my hon. friend (Sir. Sproule) will allow me to interrupt him. Wood under water, instead of decaying becomes harder and harder.
All kinds of wood ?
All kinds of wood-that is the teaching of experience.
The contract is to be let at once, and the hon. gentleman expects to have the work done at the end of the present season ?
Yes.

Will the entrance to the canal be deepened and widened so that liavi-Hon. Mr. TARTE.
gabion can be carried on successfully there ? And what provision will lie made at the end of that time for the traffic ? Is the hon. gentleman building elevators for the grain '!
No.
Will any provision be made this season ?

That is a question of policy which I would not like to discuss to-night, as we are not providing for it in the estimates. Sly own personal opinion is the same as that I expressed three years ago-that the government should provide elevators in harbours that we build ourselves. Take Port Col-borne, for instance; or let us take Slontreal. In Montreal we are to have a public elevator, because the harbour commissioners are trustees for the government and for the commercial community. Sly own opinion is that an elevator should be a public work as much as a pier or a breakwater. I know my views are not shared by everybody. So far, we have not built elevators ourselves except at St. John and Halifax in connection with the Intercolonial Railway. Private enterprise has supplied elevators on the lakes, for instance, at Collingwood, Sleaford, Owen Sound, Midland. But in respect of canals, they are our national property, and tlie question is whether we ought to build elevators on the canals. Time will tell. If private enterprise can do it, well and good. Speaking lor myself alone- because I lmvo no authority from my colleagues to say this-I believe it would be better for the government to own the terminal facilities where they own the works; in other words, at Port Colborne I think it would be better for us to own the elevators so as to be able to control the rates. Sly own opinion is that when we are fully equipped in Montreal, Quebec and St. John-I speak of the main points-our system of canals will be more largely used than it is at present. New ships are being built, there are two new ships under construction on the lakes to-day. Our canals will be used on a larger scale than they are now, and then if we have the control of our own routes we can control the rates. If we want to secure lower rates so as to compete successfully with our American friends we will be in a better position to do that. At the next session of parliament, if private enterprise has not solved the question, we shall have to do it ourselves. Although we have only part of the breakwater built, there are large ships going there now. M e will see during the recess what will turn up.

The hon. gentleman is like Mieawber, waiting for something to turn up. It seems that the government have not thought out any plan for solving tliis great question of transportation. It is * just as important for successful transporta-

tion to have elevators as to have harbours. There is no analogy between Port Colborne and Collingwood, Meaford, Goderich and Owen Sound, because in these places tlie railway companies have an interest in private elevators, and the towns have each of them given substantial bonuses for that purpose. Consequently, they are more likely to got elevators there than at Port Colborne. My fear is that after this very large expenditure, we will only have half the benefits resulting from it which we would naturally expect, provided the harbour was equipped with proper facilities for storing and handling grain when this dock, or wharf, or breakwater, is finished.

I share the views of my hon. friend. But when he becomes Minister of Public Works he will find out that influential as he may lie, he will not be able to do everything that he wants to do. A successful public man, must learn that the first virtue is patience and persistence.
Mr. Chairman,
Let us get through, let the item be carried.

I suppose a member of this House has a right to speak on a question that pertains to matters in his own constituency. I am not sure that the Chairman of this committee has a right to suggest that I should not make a remark in answer to the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule).

Well, the hon. member for East Grey made a suggestion that the government was building a breakwater at Port Colborne and expending a large amount of money there without any idea of bringing about a culmination of that expenditure in the interest of the country. Now, the situation is this :	A breakwater is being
built there to construct a harbour. The difficulty so far as transportation is concerned between the west and the east of Canada is that there has been no harbour at Port Colborne in which vessels could go to tranship their cargoes for our canal system. The government of Canada has spent about $100,000,000 on the Welland and St. Lawrence canals. It has been absolutely useless and it will remain useless for all time to come unless you have a satisfactory harbour at Port Colborne into which vessels can go and tranship their cargoes. So soon as you have a sufficient harbour at Port Colborne and elevators built there is not a question about it that not only' the bulk of the grain but all the grain products of the North-west Territories will come to Port Colborne to be transhipped into canal sized , boats and go to Montreal or Quebec. This is the cheapest transportation route to Europe on this continent by two or three cents-by two cents at least. Grain can be carried from Port Arthur to Montreal by the Welland canal and St. Lawrence route as cheaply as it is being carried from Buffalo to New York. The ship-owners of Canada and the United States appreciate that fact. They so thoroughly appreciate it that Mr. Wolvin, of Duluth, one of the largest shipowners in America, is putting ou a line of boats to carry grain from Buffalo to Quebec through the Welland canal. If this government will complete these harbour facilities at Port Colborne and will build elevators, and my own opinion is that the proper policy for the government to pursue would be to build elevators at Port Colborne and control the rates, the trade will certainly' pass through the Welland and St. Lawrence canals. There are certain companies, or individuals, at the present time who are looking to get the concession of building the elevators at Port Colborne and of putting on a line of boats between Tort Colborne and Montreal. My suggestion is that the government should build the elevators at Montreal and Port Colborne, control the rates and put the canals in a safe and proper condition and that if

tliey do so the products of the North-west, so far as the capabilities of that line of transportation are concerned, will go in that way. When these facilities for transportation are exhausted let us build other lines of transportation. We need, in this country, more than one transcontinental line. We cannot in Canada, in the future, carry all the products of the great North-west to the ocean by means of the Welland and St. Lawrence canals. The North-west of Canada is destined to be the greatest wheatgrowing country on earth. It will produce more grain and better grain possibly than any other country in the world. . It is not one-quarter, not one-tenth explored. The Peace river district will, within the next twenty years, produce more wheat than any person at present conceives to be possible and it is our duty to look to the future. The engineers of our canal system in the past have been looking too much to the immediate present. They built the Welland canal fifteen years ago for the navigation of fifteen years ago without looking to the future. They looked at the St. Lawrence canals on the same principle without looking to the future. Let us look to the future and have confidence in the development of the country that we own Irrespective of our political feelings and it will be better for us and better for the country. We want at Port Colborne the proper harbour facilities which the country demands. We want proper navigation through the Welland canal which. I believe, the people of the country will approve of and we should, so < far as we can, in a legitimate, economical ' way, develop the resources which we have in our country.
River Kaministiquia-dredging, $25,000.
Is that work to be done at the mouth of the river or up the river ?
From the mouth of the river up to the Canadian Pacific Railway elevafors.
I would like to ask the hon. minister if the government are going to do this work with their own dredge or are they going to do it by contract ?
I have made arrangements for a certain time for fifteen cents a yard.
Is that a contract ?
It is a contract for fifteen cents a yard.

That is not the best way of making a contract I .made the inquiry because I was not aware whether the gov-erenment had any dredges on Lake Superior that are available for doing this work. I wish to say that I had a letter from a gentleman in Duluth some time ago saying that he had one or two very fine dredges and he understood that the hon.
minister required dredges very badly and that he would be glad if he could make an arrangement with him to do some dredging anywhere on the upper lakes.

We were obliged to employ an American dredge at that very spot last year. We were paying fifteen and one-half cents a yard then, but this year we are giving 15 cents a yard. There were large shipments of grain being made, there was not enough water for the vessels to get up to the elevators, and I made the arrangements which I have mentioned a week or so ago.

I will let my hon. friend have the letter so that if he should desire to communicate with the gentleman that I have referred to he can do so.
St. Hyaei.ithe public building, $12,000.
The building there has become too small, and it is necessary to make that addition.
Are these works to be done by tender ?
Are you branching out with another post office in Montreal the same as in Toronto ?
We lia-ve either to enlarge the main building or to branch out. The Postmaster General has made up his mind that he can give a better service with these branches.
And you will not have to buy automobiles ?

We will get along without them in Montreal.
Valleyfield public building, $10,000.

Valleyfield is a thriving city with a population of 12,000, and in a couple of years it will have over 15,000. It is one of the most thriving little towns in the province of Quebec. It has no public building now at all. Last year parliament was good enough to allow me to have a sum in the estimates which I did not employ, but next year I intend to go on with the work. I have another vote for $10,000 for this in the main estimates.
Why do you put $10,000 in the main estimates and $10,000 in the supplementary estimates ?
It might have been better if I had put the two together, but I did not do it.
I know the hon. gentleman did not do it, but what I want to know is why he did not do it ?
If it had been in the estimates a month ago it would not have helped me at all.
That is very convincing, but I would like to know whether the hon. gentleman did much canvassing on this building in the late election in Beauharnois ?

1 used just the ordinary convincing argument that public meii use on such occasions. The $10,000 were in the estimates and the people knew I would build it. I did not make any promises. Now that the election is over I want to go on with the work.

I suppose the hon. gentleman drew then- attention to the fact that they needed it very badly, and of course by implication gave them to understand that if they elected his candidate he would go on and build it.

Joking apart, this building is very much needed.
Toronto post office-building for branch office in west end of city, $20,000.
Was there not an item already in the estimates for this building ?	*
We have $15,000 in the main estimates ; but since then we have bought a site. We will spend about $35,000. The work is under way now.
Will that complete the building ?

Yes.
Ottawa post office and custom house,. $20,500.

When these alterations are completed, we will save a rental of $1,000 a year, which we are now paying for the Customs Department on Sparks street.
Ottawa public buildings-Repairs to masonry wall, $6,500.
Mr. BORDEN Halifax). What building is that ?

It is to repair the wall of the eastern block, which is falling, just as a wall in the western block threatened to do three years ago. I was very much surprised to see how light the walls of these buildings are.
How is this work done- by contract or by day labour ?

These repairs cannot be done by contract. They are carried on under the chief architect.
Rideau Hall, Ottawa-Drain from Government House to city sewer, $7,500.
Was there never a drain there before ?

it,1C WORKS. No, the old drain is choked. We are going to change the whole system and have the drainage of Rideau Hall and grounds carried to the main sewer which has been built by the Ottawa Improvement Commission.
Toronto post office-alterations and additions,
The post office in Toronto Is in a dilapidated condition.
If the minister decided that certain repairs were necessary, why did he not have votes for them all put in the main estimates ?

The policy of the Public Works Department in the past has been to have all new works and repairs which are not begun placed in the supplementary estimates. Whether that is a good policy or not I do not know. I would rather have my main estimates include everything.

One reason for this is that the main estimates are prepared in December or January, and three or four months later we are in a better position to determine how much money we can allow for these expenditures.
Am I correct in believing that there are new works in the main estimates ?

Not one.
Toronto Junction public building-additional amount, $5,000.
Will that complete it ?
I cannot say. The contract is not yet awarded. The previous amount voted was $5,000.
What is the site likely to cost?
I do not expect to pay more than $3,000 or $4,000 for the site.
I suppose this is to carry out the understanding between the hon. gentleman and the electors at the time he was helping Mr. Campbell ?

My hon. friend attributes to me motives which never came to my mind. That amount was in the estimates when Mr. Clarke Wallace was in his seat.
Hamilton'-Examining warehouse extension,
Why this expenditure ?

The public building has become too small, and the business cannot be carried on longer in it. I am obliged to give an extension.
St. Catharines drill hall, $10,000.
What is the cost going to be ?

I do not expect to be obliged to spend more than $40,000. The site has been given to us, and all parties are agreed that the site chosen lately is satisfactory. I cannot say positively wjiat the cost will be as there may be heating or something like that to be done, but we will try to do the right thiug.
I suppose it will be between $40,000 and $50,000 ?

Yes.
Some resolutions reported.

In moving the adjournment I wish to say that there has been some conversation among members as to the desirability of our giving some-time to-morrow to private Bills. I think that that can be arranged. I had a conversation with the hon. leader of the opposition, who is equally desirous that some time should be given, but I prefer not making any definite arrangement until the right hon. the Prime Minister is in his seat. We can arrange to give some time to private Bills either to-morrow or Monday.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext: There is a very large number of Bills on the Order papersomething like twenty'. It would seem undesirable that the expense incurred should be lost to the parties simply for lack of time this session to pass the Bills. When the government took Monday, some time ago, I mentioned that I thought a longer time would be necessary for private Bills, but they did not share that opinion. They were not sufficiently impressed with the number that would probably come before the House. A portion of to-morrow or Monday should be taken, and I would support a proposition to that effect. I should suppose, in view of the necessary work to be done on a number of Bills, in the committee, that it would be desirable to assign a portion of to-morrow rather than Monday, but that is a matter of arrangement. Apart from the private Bills, what government business are we likely to have to-morrow ?
We shall proceed in Supply with the estimates of the Minister of Public Works.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 12.35 a.m. Saturday.
Saturday, May 10, 1902.
